title: ICYMI: City & State Highlights Senator Gillibrand’s Leadership During Historic Midterm Cycle For Democrats
text:
*** Read City & State’s Full Article Here***

In case you missed it, City & State published an article highlighting U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand’s leadership of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee during the 2026 cycle, in which Democrats flipped at least eight seats in last week’s midterms and cemented a Democratic Senate majority.

In the story, Senator Gillibrand credited Democrats’ laser focus on lowering costs for American families as a key to the sweeping Election Day victory, and she said that the new Democratic Congress must continue to focus on affordability and expanding healthcare access if the party is to build on its success in 2028.

Read the full City & State story here or below: 

Kirsten Gillibrand’s leadership lessons

After flipping at least seven Senate seats, the DSCC chair wants to stay in Democratic leadership.

John Celock | November 10, 2026

While remaining coy on her exact long term plans, U.S. Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand wants to remain as part of the Democratic leadership team in the Senate, after last week’s “blue tsunami.”

Gillibrand hopes to stay on as the chair of the Democratic Senate Campaign Committee for a second term following an Election Day that exceeded even the Democrats’ most optimistic assumptions. The party picked up at least seven seats in the upper chamber, with two more outstanding but leaning Democratic. It recalls 2006, when U.S. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer led Senate Democrats to a majority, helmed the DSCC for a second term and later became the party’s Senate leader.

“I do. I definitely want to be part of our leadership going forward,” Gillibrand told City & State when asked if she wanted to run for the leadership in the future. “I want to be a voice to get commonsense things done that help the American people. And so I hope that I can keep building my capabilities and building my ability to help people by doing politics well. And hopefully, I can continue to lead through that process.”

Asked specifically about the possibility of following Schumer’s path to the top Democratic job in the Senate, Gillibrand was more coy. “I will look at all opportunities for sure,” she said. 

Of course, that would mean holding her seat, when she’s up for reelection in 2030 – far from a sure thing in New York, where an emboldened progressive movement is itching to take her out. 

The DSCC chair is appointed by the Democratic leader, not elected by the full Democratic caucus – which means the only one she needs to convince is Schumer (assuming he’s reelected as leader). Gillibrand said one reason she wants to stay on at the DSCC is because the job gives her a seat at the Democratic leadership table, enabling her to help set the party’s agenda and message as they retake the majority for the second half of the current Trump presidency.

Under Gillibrand’s leadership, the DSCC raised $200 million and opened up new Senate opportunities that had not been anticipated – from Kansas to Mississippi.

Gillibrand sees a lot of similarities between the current midterms cycle and the one Schumer led two decades ago. It was then, amid a similar climate of economic distress and overseas wars (then, in Iraq; now, in Iran) that Gillibrand first made it to Congress, flipping a Republican-leaning congressional seat in 2006 before being reelected in2008 and then appointed to the U.S. Senate in 2009. 

“I think I’m uniquely positioned to understand what it takes to win red and purple places because of my own experience,” she said. “So I want to continue to do this work. I want to do it for the caucus. I want to do it for the country, and I want to help people.”

Colm O’Comartun, a national political strategist who runs 50 State, described roles like the DSCC chair as high-risk and high-reward for an ambitious politician like Gillibrand – who launched, and soon dropped, a presidential campaign ahead of 2020. She can bask in the glory of a wave election like this year, but will also take the blame if the party does not do as well going forward. 

“I think it’s a great sign that she’s somebody who’s really interested in helping her caucus and and helping build a team and a bench and in some ways thankless job, and hopefully she’ll be able to get something miraculous, which is two of these difficult years in a row (because) these these maps aren’t easy for Democrats,” he said. 

O’Comartum, a former executive director of the Democratic Governors Association, said two terms at the DSCC could position Gillibrand well for a future leadership bid. He said the 59-year-old Gillibrand could take advantage of the call for generational change in the Democratic ranks and easily build relationships with the younger Senate generation in the party by campaigning with them and positioning them to get to Washington. 

“There’s every reason to believe that she’s just at the right age to assume leadership, and will have a better relationship through her campaigning with these new members than maybe some others,” he said. 

Last September, Gillibrand predicted to City & State that Mississippi would be a 2026 U.S. Senate battleground – an idea that at the time seemed borderline-delusional. But Gillibrand would prove eerily accurate; in Mississippi, Democratic challenger Scott Colom now narrowly leads Republican U.S. Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in a race that still hasn’t been called. 

Gillibrand said that she became intrigued by Colom’s candidacy after meeting him and hearing about how Hyde-Smith blocked his bid to become a federal judge. She said data from previous elections suggested a Black Democrat had the potential to do well in the state. Recalling how Georgia Democrats had flipped two Senate seats in a fellow southern state in 2020 and thinking back to her own 2006 congressional run in a ruby-red district, she could see a pathway in a state that Democrats traditionally wrote off. 

“I wasn’t daunted that it was R+23 because, again, my district hadn’t been Democrat since Nixon, and so I thought, this is just like my election, just on a Senate-wide basis in a red state that needs to be organized just like Georgia. And if we start putting the time and effort in (and) have the best kind of candidate possible, everything is in play, and it was,” she said. 

Looking ahead to 2028, Gillibrand sees opportunities for Democrats in some of the same states that helped to fuel this year’s blue wave, including North Carolina, South Carolina, Kansas and Iowa (all of which just flipped U.S. Senate seats to the Democrats), along with Wisconsin (where Democrats swept statewide offices and picked up congressional seats), and Alaska (where Democrats lead in still-uncalled Senate and gubernatorial races). She indicated that North Carolina and Wisconsin will be top targets given the Democratic registration numbers. 

Gillibrand said the key will be for the new Democratic Congress to focus on the issues that fueled this year’s victories like affordability and healthcare, particularly Medicare. She added that new members in Republican-leaning and swing districts need to better communicate Democratic accomplishments over the next two years. By New York standards,Gillibrand is ideologically a moderate, and although she does not believe Republicans will be able to weaponize the new crop of democratic socialist electeds against the Democratic Party, she does want to caution the party against tacking too far to the left, which she blames for its 2008 losses.

She attributed the victories of leftist leaders Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Michigan U.S. Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed to their focus on affordability over unrealistic and alienating progressive policies. “They ran on costs. They made costs a cool message. They brought in new voters. Young people were excited about their youth, and that’s exciting.” she said. “They were on message. Do not get that confused. They were on message on the economic priorities and concerns of everyday voters across the country.”

###

The post ICYMI: City & State Highlights Senator Gillibrand’s Leadership During Historic Midterm Cycle For Democrats appeared first on Kirsten Gillibrand | U.S. Senator for New York.

title: Gillibrand, Colleagues Introduce Bill To Lower Age Of Medicare Eligibility To 50, Bring Down Healthcare Costs
text:
Medicare At 50 Act Would Give More Than 58 Million Americans Ages 50 To 64 Another Option For Affordable Healthcare

Today, U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY) joined nine of her Senate colleagues to introduce the Medicare at 50 Act, legislation to lower the Medicare eligibility age to 50 and allow Americans ages 50 to 64 to buy into Medicare. As Americans list the cost of healthcare as a top concern, the bill would expand access to affordable healthcare and give more than 58 million Americans more coverage options.

“Under President Trump, Americans nearing retirement are being forced to choose between paying for lifesaving care and simply being able to afford a life,” said Senator Gillibrand. “The Medicare at 50 Act would provide the security and support of Medicare years earlier to millions of aging Americans, lowering their healthcare costs and helping them save for retirement. As the top Democrat on the Senate Aging Committee, I am proud to support this important legislation, and I will continue fighting to expand access to quality and affordable care for older Americans.”

More than 60 million Americans are between the ages of 50 and 64, a population that faces significant challenges accessing affordable, comprehensive health insurance. While the Affordable Care Act (ACA) expanded access to coverage, millions of older Americans continue to face high premiums, out-of-pocket costs, and limited coverage options. Today, 11.5% of Americans between the ages of 55 and 64 remain uninsured. 

President Trump and Republicans have made matters worse with sweeping healthcare cuts in their Big Ugly Bill and their refusal to extend the ACA’s enhanced premium tax credits, driving up costs for older Americans who purchase insurance through the ACA Marketplace.

The Medicare at 50 Act would help close this gap and give Americans between the ages of 50 and 64 the option to buy into Medicare before reaching the traditional eligibility age of 65. Individuals who choose to enroll would receive the same benefits and protections available under Medicare Parts A, B, and D, including the option to enroll in a Medicare Advantage plan. The legislation would also allow eligible individuals to receive the same premium tax credits and cost-sharing subsidies they would qualify for through the ACA Marketplace, helping make coverage more affordable.

Senator Gillibrand has long fought to lower healthcare costs for older Americans and to protect Medicare access. This year, she introduced the Medicare Cost Cap Act to cap out-of-pocket costs for seniors with Medicare, and she demanded an end to the Trump administration’s WISeR program that allows for AI-driven Medicare denials. Last year, she pressed Republicans to extend the enhanced ACA premium tax credits that helped millions of Americans afford coverage. 

In addition to Senator Gillibrand, the bill is co-sponsored by Senators Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), Jeff Merkley (D-OR), Chris Van Hollen (D-MD), Jack Reed (D-RI), Tammy Duckworth (D-IL), Andy Kim (D-NJ), Cory Booker (D-NJ), Ed Markey (D-MA) and Tammy Baldwin (D-WI).

Full text of the bill is available here.

title: Gillibrand Statement On Deadly Brooklyn Building Collapse
text:

title: Gillibrand Holds Press Conference On Her Priorities For A Democratic Senate Majority
text:
Today, U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY) held a press conference to lay out her legislative priorities for a Democratic Senate majority.

The press conference follows historic Democratic gains she fought for as chair of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC) in the midterm elections, during which both the House and the Senate flipped from Republican to Democratic control. With this new majority, Senator Gillibrand is focused on lowering costs and bringing relief to working Americans who have struggled to make ends meet under the Republican trifecta.

“Last week, voters across the country made clear that they are ready for change. But the real work is just beginning,” said Senator Gillibrand. “With a Democratic Senate majority, I am laser-focused on lowering costs to bring much-needed relief to working Americans who have struggled to make ends meet under the Republican trifecta. That starts with ending the war with Iran, halting President Trump’s tariffs, making healthcare more affordable, protecting Social Security, developing commonsense guardrails for artificial intelligence, and combating Trump administration corruption.”

Gillibrand’s top priorities for the Democratic majority include:

Ending the war with Iran: Gas prices in New York are over 40 percent higher today than they were at the start of the war more than eight months ago. Ending the war with Iran is critical to get these prices under control. Gillibrand has voted 14 times on War Powers Resolutions to end the war with Iran.

Halting President Trump’s tariffs: Gillibrand’s Banning Antiquated Duties and Delivering Equitable American Levies (BAD DEAL) Act would repeal all tariffs levied under Section 338 of the Tariff Act and refund Americans for all duties paid under this authority. This includes President Trump’s 50% tariffs on Canada, which are driving up costs in New York.

Restoring access to healthcare and bringing down healthcare costs: Gillibrand cosponsors myriad legislation to restore access to healthcare and lower healthcare costs, including the Health Care Affordability Act, which would restore and permanently extend the enhanced premium tax credits offered for Affordable Care Act marketplace plans. She also supports legislation to reverse Republicans’ Medicaid cuts made through President Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act, restore coverage under New York’s Essential Plan, expand Medicare eligibility to individuals under 65, and cap prescription drug costs.

Developing commonsense guardrails for artificial intelligence: Gillibrand introduced the Secure and Accountable Military AI Act, which would impose strong restrictions on certain uses of AI by the Department of Defense, including by banning the use of AI to launch nuclear weapons.

Protecting Social Security: If Congress does not act, seniors could see their Social Security benefits cut by about 20% in just six years. Gillibrand’s Social Security Expansion Act would extend the solvency of Social Security for 75 years by requiring the wealthiest American households to pay their fair share of payroll taxes.

Combating Trump administration corruption: Gillibrand’s No Stock Act would ban senior government officials, including members of Congress, the president, the vice president, Supreme Court justices, and their spouses and dependents, from holding or trading covered financial assets.

###

The post Gillibrand Holds Press Conference On Her Priorities For A Democratic Senate Majority appeared first on Kirsten Gillibrand | U.S. Senator for New York.

title: Ahead Of Veterans Day, Gillibrand, Goodlander Introduce Bill To Bolster Research On Gender-Specific Burn Pit Health Effects
text:
Today, U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY), member of the Senate Armed Services Committee and the Senate Appropriations Military Construction, Veterans Affairs, and Related Agencies Subcommittee, and Congresswoman Maggie Goodlander (D-NH-02), member of the House Armed Services Committee and the House Veterans’ Affairs Committee, introduced the Toxic Exposure and Women Veterans’ Health Outcomes Act to improve research on burn pits’ effects on women veterans’ health. 

The bill would require the Departments of Veterans Affairs (VA) and Defense (DoD) to examine the understudied linkages between military service near burn pits and gender-specific health outcomes for women veterans, such as impacts on fertility and the prevalence of birth defects in babies born to affected women. The ultimate goal of the bill would be to justify the addition of more women-specific health conditions to the PACT Act and to provide women veterans with insight into the conditions their children may have as a result of their toxic exposure.

“I was proud to pass the PACT Act in 2022 to deliver on our country’s promise to take care of our toxic-exposed veterans. But our work is not over,” said Senator Gillibrand. “The VA must conduct more research into the effects of burn pits on our brave women veterans so we can make sure their conditions are adequately covered. It is absolutely imperative that we fill in these gaps in our data and give women veterans access to the full spectrum of care and benefits they deserve.”

“The women of America’s Armed Forces breathed the same toxic burn pit smoke as their brothers in arms. They deserve the same answers,” said Congresswoman Goodlander, a member of both the House Armed Services and Veterans’ Affairs Committees who served for more than a decade as an intelligence officer in the United States Navy Reserve. 

“Instead, too many women who served our country in uniform are still left wondering whether their service cost them their health, their fertility, or the health of their children. That’s dead wrong, and Congress can fix it now. I’m proud to join Senator Gillibrand in leading this bill to close these research gaps and make sure no woman who served our country is left behind. Our veterans have always had our backs. We have a sacred obligation to have theirs.”

The Toxic Exposure and Women Veterans’ Health Outcomes Act would direct the VA, in collaboration with DoD, to conduct a comprehensive study on burn-pit related health effects experienced by women veterans. This would include:

Effects on female reproductive capacity and reproductive organs;

Effects on reproductive outcomes, including birth defects, adverse reproductive outcomes, and fertility;

Effects on developmental disabilities of the children of covered individuals;

Effects on female-specific organs and tissues; and

Other effects unique to the physiology of women.

More than two decades ago, a landmark study found that women veterans from the Vietnam War faced a significantly elevated risk of having children with moderate to severe birth defects. As a result of the study, in 2000, Congress mandated that children of female Vietnam-era veterans receive presumptive VA benefits if they are born with certain birth defects. However, despite this evidence and numerous other studies documenting the harmful effects of toxic exposures in post-9/11 veterans, research on reproductive health and birth outcomes for the over 300,000 women who served in post-9/11 conflicts remains severely limited.

“We know through our members’ stories and our own personal experiences that female service members are at extreme risk of developing toxic exposure-related health conditions, including those related to reproductive healthcare. Because these conditions are often unique to or manifest differently in women, and can remain undetected for years or even decades, DoD and the VA have struggled to fully understand the scope of these health impacts and ensure women veterans receive the recognition, care, and treatment they deserve,” said Dr. Kyleanne Hunter, CEO of IAVA. “We are thrilled with Senator Gillibrand’s introduction of the Toxic Exposure and Reproductive Health Outcomes Act, which would finally require a holistic look at the impacts of toxic exposure on women to close longstanding gaps in research, improve health outcomes, and ensure women veterans are no longer overlooked.”

“The Tragedy Assistance Program for Survivors (TAPS) is grateful to Senator Gillibrand for introducing the Toxic Exposure and Women Veterans’ Health Outcomes Act,” said Bonnie Carroll, TAPS President and Founder. “This important legislation will address long overdue gaps in care and research for women veterans exposed to burn pits and toxic substances during military service. TAPS is proud to support this legislation and looks forward to its passage.” 

“Reproductive health problems after deployment are under-studied and too easily overlooked,” said Julie Tomaska, PhD, retired Air Force, Chief Scientific Officer Burn Pits 360. “For a woman veteran exposed to burn pit smoke, facing infertility, pregnancy loss, or a child’s birth defect is hard enough without wondering whether her service played a role. After Congress required VA to study women who served in Vietnam, researchers found a significantly higher risk of birth defects in their children, and those conditions are now covered. Yet for the nearly 300,000 women who served after 9/11, only two studies have examined birth outcomes. Senator Gillibrand’s bill closes that gap, building the evidence needed to recognize these conditions under the PACT Act.”

“Women veterans deserve the same recognition, research, and care for service-connected toxic exposures as their male counterparts,” said Jessica Jordan, Executive Director of Military Veterans Advocacy Inc. “This legislation represents an important step toward understanding the long-term health effects of toxic exposure on women veterans and their families. MVA strongly supports this initiative and urges Congress to advance this important legislation.”

Gillibrand was a leading champion of the PACT Act, which was signed by President Biden in 2022. The PACT Act expanded healthcare and benefits for veterans suffering from illnesses caused by exposure to burn pits and other toxic substances while serving abroad in post-9/11 conflicts. These burn pit-related medical conditions are now presumptively service-connected, meaning that veterans who were deployed overseas near burn pits no longer have to provide direct proof that their disease is service-related in order to receive benefits.

The Toxic Exposure and Women Veterans’ Health Outcomes Act is endorsed by Iraq and Afghanistan Veterans of America (IAVA), the Tragedy Assistance Program for Survivors (TAPS), the National Military Family Association (NMFA), Burn Pits 360, Military Veterans Advocacy Inc. (MVA), the Wounded Warrior Project, League of United Latin American Citizens (LULAC), Tri-State Women Warriors, and the American Legion.

The full text of the Toxic Exposure and Women Veterans’ Health Outcomes Act can be found here.

A video of Senator Gillibrand discussing the bill can be found here.

###

The post Ahead Of Veterans Day, Gillibrand, Goodlander Introduce Bill To Bolster Research On Gender-Specific Burn Pit Health Effects appeared first on Kirsten Gillibrand | U.S. Senator for New York.

title: Gillibrand Addresses Stephen Miller Chief Of Staff News, Says Democrats Must Focus On Lowering Costs, Ending Iran War On MS NOW’s Politicsnation With Al Sharpton
text:
Gillibrand: “People Were Fed Up With Trump’s Corruption And Chaos And High Costs. They Voted For Change. And So This Congress And In The U.S. Senate, We’re Going To Focus On Exactly What The American People Asked Us To Do.”

***Hear Senator Gillibrand’s Full Interview Here***

U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand appeared on MS NOW’s PoliticsNation with Al Sharpton to discuss Democrats’ plan to bring down the cost of living and deliver much-needed relief for working Americans under their newfound Senate majority. 

She highlighted her party’s laser focus on lowering costs for American families, including by ending the Iran war, restoring access to healthcare, and holding the president accountable for his corruption and his prioritization of vanity projects over the wellbeing of American families.

Senator Gillibrand also addressed the president’s promotion of Stephen Miller to chief of staff and threats to veto commonsense legislation next Congress: 

“[President Trump] did put in place the architecture of this culture of corruption and chaos and high costs in putting Stephen Miller as chief of staff, so he does not seem positioned to be listening to the American people to get stuff done. But that’s not going to daunt. It’s not going to stop us. We’re going to work on getting all those costs down by passing commonsense legislation. And if President Trump dares to veto restoring Medicaid, covering dental and vision and hearing, getting costs for medicines down – if he dares to veto things that get the cost of groceries and housing and fuel costs down, he will – his party will lose even bigger in ‘28.”

Watch Senator Gillibrand’s interview with Reverend Al Sharpton here. Full transcript of Senator Gillibrand’s interview below:

REV. AL SHARPTON: Senator, you said Democrats now have to end the war in Iran, lower cost, and hold President Trump accountable. What does that actually look like when you take control in January?

GILLIBRAND: Well, Reverend, as you said, this election was about change. People were fed up with Trump’s corruption and chaos and high costs. They voted for change, and so this Congress and in the U.S. Senate, we’re going to focus on exactly what the American people asked us to do. We’re going to try to get our healthcare costs down, make sure prescription drugs are more affordable, make sure people have access. Trump cut millions off of Medicaid. Make sure our seniors can get dental, vision, and hearing. So get costs down and make it more accessible, more affordable. Focus on food costs. Focus on housing costs. Focus on fuel costs. The war in Iran has driven up all of those costs, and it’s unauthorized. It’s illegal. The American people don’t want it. It is deeply unpopular. So we need to end the war to get those costs down, and address the chaotic tariffs, which are also keeping food costs and housing costs and medicine costs high. So we have to right the ship, get costs down, and hold this president accountable for his corruption and the chaos that he created across this country.

SHARPTON: Senator, President Trump is already calling himself Mr. Veto. And after losing Congress, he responded by putting Stephen Miller in charge of the White House. Not exactly a signal that he’s looking for compromise. How do you govern with a president who appears ready to fight you at every turn?

GILLIBRAND: Well, it’s true. President Trump does have his little veto cap, and he has threatened to use it. And he did put in place the architecture of this culture of corruption and chaos and high costs in putting Stephen Miller as chief of staff. So he does not seem positioned to be listening to the American people to get stuff done. But that’s not going to daunt, it’s not going to stop us. We’re going to work on getting all those costs down by passing commonsense legislation. And if President Trump dares to veto restoring Medicaid, covering dental and vision and hearing, getting costs for medicines down – if he dares to veto things that get the cost of groceries and housing and fuel costs down, he will – his party will lose even bigger in ‘28.

SHARPTON: Now, Senator, you and Senator Chuck Schumer deserve a lot of credit for what happened Tuesday. He helped recruit candidates like Roy Cooper and Sherrod Brown, and you, as a DSCC chair, helped build a map that expanded into states Democrats weren’t supposed to win. But there’s still a real debate about who should lead this new majority. At least five incoming Democratic senators have said they won’t support Schumer or want new leadership, and others still haven’t committed. What’s your view on this?

GILLIBRAND: Well, first of all, it really was a blue tsunami. I mean, the weight of what was accomplished is so significant. Our candidates were so brilliant; they understood exactly what was at stake in this election by listening to voters. And we have won seven Senate seats, and we are likely to win two more. And of those seven, five are in states that Donald Trump won by double digits. So I think people are grateful for the hard work that our candidates did, being on message, campaigning constantly, being in their communities, talking about costs and talking about solutions. And I think they’re grateful for Senator Schumer’s hard work in not only helping to marshal these incredible candidates, but raising them the resources they need to win. We were outspent astronomically by the Republicans because they had so many super PACs and so many billionaires. But our individual candidates went toe to toe with every one of their opponents and were able to communicate effectively. And that credit really has to go to Senator Schumer as well as all these incredible candidates that really got this done.

SHARPTON: Senator, as DSCC chair, you have to feel pretty good about this map. Democrats won states that Donald Trump, as you said, carried by double digits. But success also created different problems late in the race. Places that had been considered long shots became competitive. Angie Nixon lost Florida by less than three points. Jamie Davis lost Louisiana by less than two, and Scott Colom is still in a razor-thin race in Mississippi. This isn’t about second-guessing every spending decision, but is there a lesson here about expanding the map earlier and taking some of these red state candidates seriously sooner. What might the party do differently next time?

GILLIBRAND: Well, just so you know, we did take these candidates very seriously. I’ve been working with Scott Colom for over a year and a half. He’s come to a bunch of our big events nationally. Our supporters across the country got to know him. We invested $8 million early to register new voters in Mississippi. So Scott has been on our radar for a very, very long time, and so we were always trying to double down to expand the map. We had four expansion states, and we won three out of four. It was Mississippi, it was Kansas, it was South Carolina and Florida. And of the four states, Angie’s state just happened to be the most expensive. It is a behemoth of a state. It is deeply red. But it is a testament to her candidacy, her unbelievable, inspiring candidacy that she organized her state. She had a very late primary, and she still got her vote out. She ran an incredible race. We’ve always taken her seriously. I’ve personally done fundraisers for her, and she really hit the ground running. But what it does tell us is that all of these states are going to be in play next cycle. We have another shot at Florida next cycle. We have another shot at North Carolina next cycle. And we have Wisconsin. So we have so many opportunities for the next cycle to continue to build on this map to continue to raise the kind of money that allows us to keep expanding. Again, to win five states that Trump won with double digits, you will add to that two more if we win, and when we win, let’s just say, when we win Mississippi and Alaska because we are up in both of those states.

SHARPTON: All right, Kirsten Gillibrand. Always good to be with, have you with us, and to be talking to you. New York senator and chair of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee. Thank you. 

###

title: Gillibrand, Schumer Announce Nearly $2 Million In USDA Funding For New York State
text:
Today, U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand, a member of the Senate Appropriations Agriculture and Rural Development Subcommittee, and U.S. Senator Chuck Schumer announced $1,915,024 in U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) grants for New York State. This federal funding will support New York’s ongoing efforts to connect farmers with customers and make food more affordable. The funding is distributed through the Farmers Market Promotion Program (FMPP) and Local Food Promotion Program (LFPP) grant programs. Of these funds, more than $1.1 million is dedicated to local food promotion programs, and more than $700,000 will fund farmers market food promotion programs.

“As New York continues to expand access to healthy food while SNAP benefits are being targeted by the Trump administration, I am proud to secure these federal dollars for both urban and rural communities,” said Senator Gillibrand. “These grants will be used to expand the reach of local food programs and farms, boosting regional economies and helping to ensure New Yorkers can eat healthfully. I will keep pushing for funding that helps New Yorkers afford sustainable, regionally sourced ingredients.”

“I’m proud to deliver nearly $2 million in federal funding to support food programs and farmers across New York,” said Senator Schumer. “As cruel Trump administration SNAP cuts begin to take effect, this funding will help make healthy, locally-grown food more accessible and affordable. I will always fight to support our farmers, strengthen rural communities, and keep food on the table for New York families.”

The offices of Senator Gillibrand and Schumer will continue surveillance over the issuing of these grants to ensure they are administered efficiently to their recipients.

RecipientCityAllocationProject Description

Farm to People LLC.Brooklyn$500,000This project will bolster a proven supply chain, expanding aggregation capacity and producer access on the Finger Lakes-to-New York City corridor for farms that cannot affordably access the NYC market on their own.

title: Gillibrand Underscores Democrats’ Commitment To Lower Costs, End Iran War, Hold Trump Accountable On NPR’s Morning Edition
text:
Gillibrand: “Our Goal Is To Meet The Needs Of The American People. We Are Going To Focus Laser-Like On Getting Their Costs Down.”

***Hear Senator Gillibrand’s Full Interview Here***

Today, U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand appeared on NPR’s Morning Edition to discuss Democrats’ historic sweep of the midterm elections and their plan to deliver for the American people with their newfound majorities. 

She highlighted Democrats’ focus on lowering costs for American families, including by ending the Iran war, undoing President Trump’s tariffs, and restoring access to healthcare, as well as holding the president accountable for his corruption and his prioritization of vanity projects over the wellbeing of American families. 

Senator Gillibrand also addressed the president’s threats to veto commonsense legislation head on:

“[President Trump]’s got his little veto cap. But as you’ve seen, he’s much more focused on the Reflecting Pool and his ballroom than anything else right now. So I don’t know what to expect out of this president. But if we have a bill that is bipartisan to restore healthcare for the people who lost their Medicaid or improve access to affordable medicines and other things, like, I dare him to veto that.”

Listen to Senator Gillibrand’s interview with NPR here. Full transcript of Senator Gillibrand’s interview below:

A MARTÍNEZ: For more about what’s next for Democrats in Congress, New York Senator Kirsten Gillibrand joins us now. She chairs the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee. Senator, on its website, the DSCC says its purpose is electing a Democratic Senate through organizing, fundraising, and candidate recruitment. It sounds like you went three for three there. What did you see after the 2024 elections that set you up for the results you got in 2026?

SENATOR GILLIBRAND: Well, I knew that the climate that President Trump was going to create would be toxic. And he just continued to double down on things the American people didn’t want. He promised no forever wars, but he got us headlong into Iran. He promised he’d get costs down for groceries and housing and energy costs, and they continue to rise because of his war in Iran and his chaotic tariffs. And his disregard for the American people just kept growing. And so with talented candidates running all across the country, they were able to have a conversation with the American people about what they want. They want groceries to be affordable. They want to be able to afford to live where they want to live. They want to be able to get healthcare for their children and families. And when President Trump goes around canceling Medicaid for families and getting rid of food stamps for families who are struggling just to feed their children, that’s the kind of actions by the president and this administration that made the climate so favorable for these inspiring candidates that then just went to the voters and talked about their vision for America and what they want to get done for the American people. 

MARTÍNEZ: So it sounds like, Senator, maybe you weren’t so surprised over the margin of victory.

GILLIBRAND: Well, I was hoping we’d win four. I really didn’t imagine we’d be winning eight or nine seats. We are now up to win nine Senate seats. All of our expansion states and all of the opportunities in these red and purple states came to fruition because these candidates were so transformational. A lot of them are the next generation, a lot of them are very authentic to their states. You look at Mary Peltola who ran on fish, family, and freedom. You look at somebody like Scott Colom, who’s a local DA in red, red Mississippi, really taking it to his community about his vision for his community and what he wants to do to bring down costs and provide opportunity for those families. Those candidacies resonated, and that is why we are seeing unbelievable returns in states that Democrats haven’t had for decades. 

MARTÍNEZ: So with control in the House and the Senate, will Democrats try to impeach President Trump again?

GILLIBRAND: Well, our goal is to meet the needs of the American people. We are going to focus laser-like on getting their costs down. We have to end this war in Iran, which is driving up fuel and diesel, and every supply chain problem that’s driving up costs for everything. We have to deal with these chaotic tariffs and get them down because they’re driving up food costs and housing costs and everyday goods costs. And we have to restore access to healthcare. People literally lost – millions of Americans lost their healthcare. So we need to make sure Medicare and Medicaid are strengthened. We need to improve people’s healthcare. Our healthcare system in America isn’t that great. And so we need to make sure people can get hearing and dental and be able to actually get the medicines that their doctors prescribe without breaking the bank. And so good healthcare, cheaper healthcare, better healthcare are all priorities. 

MARTÍNEZ: We hear candidates, though, talk about holding the Trump administration accountable. So what if that’s what the people want, too? They want you to kind of, walk and chew gum at the same time.

GILLIBRAND: We do want to hold the administration accountable. Yeah, no, we can do both. And one thing we could do is ban stock trading. We could say members of Congress, the administration, senior cabinet officials cannot be buying and selling stocks or cryptocurrency or anything else based on inside information and lining their own pockets. The amount of corruption in Washington, particularly around this president, is the highest I’ve ever seen. It is so incredible how much pay to play, how much fraud and corruption is within this White House. And so people don’t understand how the president has this unlimited money for his ballrooms and unlimited money for his billionaire buddies, but they don’t have enough money to pay for healthcare or to get costs for groceries down. And so they want this focus that they have to make America better for them, and don’t allow this administration continually put their own preferences and their own wealth in front of the American people. That’s the part of corruption that is infuriating voters, because they’re watching this president, like, focus on his ballroom and his triumphal arch and his airplane and not focus on their lives and allowing their children to get the healthcare they need to survive and thrive. And so it’s a choice that’s being made. And that’s what they’re so angry about. So you have to do accountability of the administration, but deliver for the American people at the same time. 

MARTÍNEZ: The reason I asked that is because I was wondering what Democratic priorities would be. So let’s hear from Texas Senator-elect James Talarico on CNN. 

TALARICO: I think our top priority has to be delivering for the people of Texas, for the people of this country. They didn’t send us to Washington for political retribution. They sent us to Washington to lower costs, to root out corruption, to get this economy back on track. And that needs to be our focus. 

MARTÍNEZ: So Senator, it sounds like you agree with him, at least a little bit on this.

GILLIBRAND: Oh, I do.

MARTÍNEZ: But how do you square that sentiment with maybe a part of the party that might say, ‘Hey, lawyer up,’ like California Congressman Robert Garcia, that’s his two-word statement. He’s gonna be House Oversight and Government Reform Committee chair.

GILLIBRAND: Well, that’s one of his jobs. He’s the head of that committee. And so people want to see that the rules of the road are real. This president has broken the Constitution, the norms, every type of law you can imagine. And people feel deeply uncomfortable that you’ve broken the country in a way that isn’t fixable. So part of our job is to begin to restore order and restore all the things that President Trump has undermined. Like, he’s cut access to healthcare, to Medicaid. He has cut access to food stamps. He’s cut NIH funding. Like, things that go into the community to help the people survive, to give them the healthcare they need, to make sure there’s resources for food and housing. So they want things fixed, and they want things that have harmed them to be reversed. And so we need to double down on providing for the American people. Just as James Talarico has said, they’re expecting that we get their costs down. They’re expecting that we make sure people have healthcare. So those are must-dos. Part of how you deliver that is holding them accountable. 

MARTÍNEZ: How do you do that if President Trump becomes Mr. Veto, as he has previewed? 

GILLIBRAND: Yeah, so he’s threatened to be Mr. Veto. He’s got his little veto cap. But as you’ve seen, he’s much more focused on the Reflecting Pool and his ballroom than anything else right now. So I don’t know what to expect out of this president. But if we have a bill that is bipartisan to restore healthcare for the people who lost their Medicaid or improve access to affordable medicines and other things, like, I dare him to veto that. I dare him to stand in front of the American people and say, ‘You don’t deserve access to healthcare.’ So, if he decides to veto the commonsense things that get groceries down or housing prices down, then ‘28’s gonna be very favorable for Democrats.

###

The post Gillibrand Underscores Democrats’ Commitment To Lower Costs, End Iran War, Hold Trump Accountable On NPR’s Morning Edition appeared first on Kirsten Gillibrand | U.S. Senator for New York.

title: Gillibrand, Schumer Demand Trump Approve Major Disaster Declaration For September Nor’easter
text:
Today, U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY) and Senator Chuck Schumer (D-NY) called on President Trump to approve Governor Hochul’s request for a Major Disaster Declaration following the September 26 and 27, 2026 nor’easter that battered downstate New York. The storm brought coastal flooding and heavy winds to Long Island and New York City, resulting in increased expenditure of state and local resources to help communities recover from the disastrous conditions. 

In a letter to President Trump, the senators underscored their support for Governor Hochul’s request for disaster relief, which would unlock Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) resources to help alleviate the financial burden that counties and the state took on to mitigate the impacts of the storm. Governor Hochul’s request included Public Assistance for Nassau and Suffolk Counties and Hazard Mitigation for the entire state. 

The senators wrote, “We support the Governor’s request for Public Assistance (PA) for Nassau and Suffolk Counties and Hazard Mitigation for the entire State. We also support the inclusion of any additional counties that New York State believes meets the threshold for PA. Such a declaration under the Robert T. Stafford Disaster Relief and Emergency Assistance Act (P.L. 100-707) would unlock crucial Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) resources.” 

The senators continued by emphasizing the disastrous nature of the storm. They wrote, “The storm battered southern New York with strong winds and heavy rain, which combined with a full moon that exacerbated high tides, caused major coastal flooding and flash flooding. In addition to the flooding, gale-force winds felled trees and branches that damaged utility poles. During the storm over 200,000 New Yorkers lost power, of which over half were on Long Island.”

The senators concluded the letter by stressing the need for federal resources to help downstate New York recover from the storm. They wrote, “The New York State Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Management, in partnership with FEMA Region 2 and Nassau and Suffolk Counties, has documented and validated that the damage and costs from this nor’easter exceed the State’s threshold for a disaster declaration.Without federal support that a Major Disaster Declaration can provide, New Yorkers in Nassau and Suffolk Counties will lose a critical partner in their efforts to recover and prepare for future natural disasters.”

The full text of the letter can be found here.

title: Gillibrand Statement On Trump Administration Plan To Undermine Workplace Protections For Pregnant Women
text:
Today, in light of reporting that the Trump administration plans to scale back job protections for pregnant women enacted as part of the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act, U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand released the following statement:

“President Trump’s continued attacks on women and families are disgraceful. Now, on top of the sky-high cost of groceries, gas, and utilities, American women will also have to worry about losing their jobs if they need accommodations for pregnancy-related issues or to take care of their reproductive health. This is yet another backwards and shortsighted move by the Trump administration that will weaken our economy, harm our families, and erode our personal liberties.”

In 2022, Congress passed the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act, which Senator Gillibrand cosponsored, as part of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2023. The law instituted the workplace protections for women affected by pregnancy, childbirth, or related medical conditions that are now under threat by the Trump administration. These accommodations can include:

Flexible scheduling for prenatal or postnatal appointments

Additional, longer, or more flexible breaks to drink water, eat, rest, or use the bathroom

Light duty, or help with manual labor and lifting

Temporary transfer to a less physically demanding or safer position

Limiting exposure to hazardous chemicals

Access to a water bottle or food

Leave or time off to recover from childbirth, even for those who don’t qualify for FMLA

Leave or time off for bedrest, recovery from miscarriage, postpartum depression, mastitis, and other pregnancy-related health issues

Providing equipment such as a stool to sit on

Changing a uniform or dress code, like allowing wearing maternity pants

Changing a work schedule, like allowing shorter work hours or a later start time to accommodate morning sickness

Breaks, private space (not in a bathroom), and other accommodations for lactation needs, like adding a lock to a meeting room for private breast milk expression

Remote work or telework

Senator Gillibrand has spent her career in Congress championing women in the workplace. In addition to consponsoring the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act, she leads the FAMILY Act, which would establish a national program guaranteeing 12 weeks of paid family and medical leave for every American. She has introduced the FAMILY Act in every Congress since 2013. She also introduced the bipartisan More Paid Leave for More Americans Act, which would establish a competitive grant program for states that provide a minimum of six weeks of parental, caregiving, or medical leave, as well as the Comprehensive Paid Leave for Federal Employees Act, which would expand federal paid leave for federal employees to include 12 weeks of family and medical leave.

title: Gillibrand, Schumer Deliver $107.7 Million For Metro-North Upgrades Along The Harlem Line
text:
Grant Was Made Possible By The Bipartisan Infrastructure Law That Gillibrand and Schumer Fought To Pass

Today, U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand, ranking member of the Senate Appropriations Subcommittee on Transportation, Housing and Urban Development, and Related Agencies (THUD), and Democratic Minority Leader Chuck Schumer announced $107,712,000 in Federal Railroad Administration (FRA) funding to eliminate a busy railroad crossing along Metro-North’s Harlem Line in New Castle, removing a crash hazard for local drivers and train passengers. The project will replace the existing ground-level intersection with a new roadway overpass, separating vehicular traffic from train tracks. Once complete, the new overpass will eliminate collision risks between cars and trains, reduce traffic delays, and improve daily commutes. Gillibrand personally wrote to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy to advocate for this critical funding.

“I am proud to deliver this critical $107 million federal investment to eliminate a dangerous rail crossing on Metro-North’s Harlem Line,” said Senator Gillibrand. “This investment, which is a direct result of the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, will improve safety and reduce commute delays, helping to keep people moving in New Castle. I will keep fighting to ensure New York’s transit networks have the resources they need to serve New Yorkers.”

“A whopping $107 million in federal funding is on track to make major safety improvements in Westchester County in New Castle and Chappaqua! I’m proud to deliver this award from my Bipartisan Infrastructure & Jobs Law to finally move forward the safety upgrades needed for the notorious Roaring Brook Road crossing in New Castle. The new overpass will eliminate the potential for accidents and ensure people and passengers can travel safely around the crossing,” said Senator Schumer. “Four years ago, I stood in Garrison alongside local leaders, first responders, railroad officials, and families who were affected by these tragic rail crossing collisions and promised to deliver federal investment in making rail crossings across the Hudson Valley safer. I fought to deliver $3 million last year to create preliminary designs, to lay the groundwork for this new major federal investment, and ensure the safety of our Hudson Valley Metro-North commuters, rail workers, pedestrians, and drivers. This is a major step forward toward putting into place effective measures that will reduce life-threatening collisions in high-risk areas.”

The funding will carry the Roaring Brook Road project through its final design phase, necessary property purchases, and full construction. Currently, the street-level crossing sees more than 9,000 vehicles and 107 passenger trains every day.

The Crossing Safety/Railroad Crossing Elimination (RCE) Grant Program at the FRA, which is providing this funding, was established under the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law signed by President Biden in 2021. RCE funds highway-rail or pathway-rail grade crossing improvement projects that focus on improving the safety and mobility of people and goods. This program invests in railroad infrastructure projects that will reduce accidents, support economic vitality that will create good-paying jobs, strengthen supply chains, and apply innovative technology.

###

title: Gillibrand Demands End To AI-Driven Medicare Denials Following Substantial Drop In Patient Services Under Pilot Program
text:
Today, U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY), ranking member of the U.S. Senate Aging Committee, issued the following statement after reports of large drops in Medicare services in the six states under the Trump administration’s WISeR pilot program, which uses artificial intelligence (AI) to deny seniors’ medical claims:

“AI has no place making the final call on Americans’ medical care. The sudden drop in Medicare services due to Trump’s AI pre-approval experiment is dangerous and unacceptable. Healthcare decisions belong between a doctor and a patient – not an algorithm.”

In May, Senator Gillibrand introduced a resolution to end the Trump administration’s experiment with the WISeR (Wasteful and Inappropriate Service Reduction) Model that allows AI to conduct prior authorization and allows third-party AI companies to profit from denying seniors’ medical claims in Traditional Medicare. Senate Republicans voted to block her legislation in July. 

The WISeR model has introduced prior authorization requirements into Traditional Medicare for a set of newly impacted health care services, letting AI decide what care patients receive even after their doctors recommend a particular procedure or medical device. The third-party AI companies involved in the program are also compensated for “averted expenditures,” rewarding those companies based on the volume or cost of care they deny to seniors on Medicare. A recent report showed that the WISeR model has been catastrophic for seniors in the six states where it has been deployed so far.

title: Gillibrand, Colleagues Sound Alarm On Trump Administration Plan To Cut Nursing Home Inspections, Putting Over 114,000 Residents At Risk
text:
U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY), ranking member of the Special Committee on Aging, pressed the Trump administration about concerns regarding the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services’ (CMS) newly implemented Risk-Based Survey (RBS) program. This policy limits the number and scope of required federal and state inspections, putting an estimated 114,300 nursing home residents in nearly 1,700 facilities at risk. CMS recently released the full list of the nursing homes that will be subjected to shorter, less rigorous reviews and inspections.

Senator Gillibrand, along with Senators Elizabeth Warren (D-MA), Mazie Hirono (D-HI), and Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), sounded the alarm about the risks of weakening inspections in a letter to CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz.

“Nursing home residents depend on comprehensive, thorough, and unannounced surveys to detect and prevent substandard care that puts their health at risk,” said Senator Gillibrand. “By weakening oversight and allowing watered-down inspections, the Trump administration is putting nursing home residents at greater risk of mistreatment, neglect, and abuse. Our seniors deserve better. As the top Democrat on the Senate Aging Committee, I am working to promote safety and quality in nursing homes across New York to ensure residents receive the care they need.”

The senators’ letter highlighted a new analysis by Consumer Voice, which showed that the criteria CMS uses to identify lower-risk facilities eligible for reduced scrutiny do not reliably reflect high-quality care. For example, Consumer Voice found that dozens of homes on the reduced survey list have had a resident abuse tag or icon on the CMS Care Compare website since September 2025 and that about half of the newly RBS-eligible nursing homes would not have been eligible a year ago — indicating that, at best, they have a very limited record of providing high-quality services.

“CMS has adopted the RBS against a broader backdrop of rolled-back nursing home standards, including the elimination of new minimum staffing standards and delays to nursing home financial transparency requirements. These actions already place nursing home residents at risk — and the new policy of limited surveys will only make matters worse,” the senators wrote in the letter.

Gillibrand and her colleagues requested that CMS release information on whether the RBS adequately protects nursing home residents and follows federal statutory requirements by November 9, 2026.

The full text of the letter can be found here.

title: Gillibrand On Iran War Costing Nearly $50 Billion, Now Lasting 8 Months
text:
Today, Trump and Republicans’ war in Iran has hit its 8-month anniversary. 

The war has now cost nearly $50 billion dollars of taxpayer money, wounded hundreds and killed at least 23 American service members, depleted our stockpile of long-range missiles, and cost New Yorkers billions in higher costs.

Over and over again, the American people have heard an endless parade of broken and shifting promises about the war from the president. We were told the war was a “total and complete victory,” “won’t be difficult,” was “projected [to last] four to five weeks,” was “winding down,” was ending “very soon,” was “ahead of schedule,” was going to end in “two or three weeks,” then “two or three days,” then “very close,” then again a “few days,” then “going to end pretty soon.” 

None of this has been true. Trump has even said the war will possibly escalate after the midterm elections. 

Trump campaigned on no new wars. In June 2025, Trump, Rubio, and Hegseth claimed the Iranian nuclear program was “obliterated.” Then the president turned around and claimed he had to start this war with Iran because they were “two weeks away” from creating a nuclear bomb. In the first months of the war, Secretary Hegseth and President Trump bragged that the Iranian military had been “decimated” and was “no longer a threat.” They said Iran’s missile program was “functionally destroyed,” with stockpiles depleted, decimated and ineffective. The White House stated that Iran’s ballistic missile arsenal had been razed. General Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, said in April, “Over the course of 38 days of major combat operation, the joint force achieved the military objectives as defined by the President.”

Yet the war has continued. 

Below is a statement on this 8-month anniversary from Senator Kirsten Gillibrand, member of the Senate Armed Services and Intelligence Committees:

“This illegal war was launched without a clear plan, executed without a coherent strategy, and now, eight months later, American families are still paying the price at the gas pump, at the grocery store, and with their tax dollars. 

“From the start, this administration has lied to the American people about the timeline, the strategy, and the cost of this war. Nearly $50 billion in taxpayer dollars has already been spent, while families face thousands of dollars in higher costs and American service members are killed and wounded.

“This costly war must end to bring relief to working families, and this administration must be held accountable for its costly failures.” 

###

title: New Report: Trump’s Wealth From Oil & Gas Stocks Climbs To As Much As $81.6 Million Amid Iran War, Surging Costs For Americans
text:
Americans Have Now Spent An Additional $101 Billion On Gas Since The Start Of Trump’s Iran War, Averaging $856 In Added Costs Per Family

This week, the Joint Economic Committee (JEC) – Minority released a new analysis finding that so far this year, President Trump’s personal wealth from oil and gas stocks has grown by as much as $35.8 million. This brings his net holdings in the sector to as much as $81.6 million and nearly doubles the oil and gas wealth the president held at the end of 2025. Trump’s war in Iran has caused oil and gas prices to skyrocket, and the Committee also found that 94% of Trump’s 2026 oil and gas stock purchases occurred after the war began, with Trump buying as much as $17.5 million in oil and gas stocks since February 28.

In response to the new report that highlights President Trump’s egregiously misplaced priorities, U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand issued the following statement:

“President Trump chose to start his Iran war knowing it was going to raise gas prices on Americans already struggling to get by,” said Senator Gillibrand. “As Americans pay more than $100 billion more at the pump, Trump is making a fortune turning the White House into his personal trading desk and saying he doesn’t ‘give a damn.’ The president must end this wasteful war and instead focus on bringing down costs for the people he was elected to serve.”

The report comes as President Trump bragged this weekend about oil and gas profits due to his war with Iran and said “I don’t give a damn” that people are suffering at the pump. The new report also includes national and state-by-state calculations that show that Americans have now spent an additional $101 billion on gas since the start of President Trump’s Iran war, which is an average of $856 in added costs per family.

Experts have observed that it is rare for presidents to hold and trade stocks in individual companies while in office, given that presidents’ actions can impact the stock market significantly. Trump, on the other hand, has purchased oil and gas stocks in major companies that have profited directly off of Trump’s decisions – including his war in Iran and his other favors to the industry.

Senator Gillibrand has been fighting back against President Trump’s moves to profit from his office at working families’ expense. Last year, she introduced the No Stock Act, which would ban the president, the vice president, members of Congress, Supreme Court justices, and their immediate families from holding or trading stocks. In February, she introduced the Financial Disclosure Modernization Act, which would increase transparency around the finances of President Trump and other senior officials by expanding disclosure reporting categories to include a new upper tier of “greater than $1 billion.” She has also been pushing to bring down the costs of the Iran war, including by urging the Trump administration to raise the federal standard mileage rate to give New Yorkers relief from sky-high gas prices.

title: ICYMI: Gillibrand Op-Ed In Empire Report: Costs Are Up. So Are The Stakes This November.
text:
Today, U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand published an opinion piece in Empire Report laying out the stakes for the midterm elections next week.

Senator Gillibrand detailed how President Trump and Republicans in Congress have raised grocery and utility costs for New York families, cut healthcare and food assistance, and waged a war that has spiked gas prices across the country. Next week, voters get to issue a referendum on this cost-increasing chaos.

The full text of the op-ed can be found here and below:

Costs are up. So are the stakes this November.
By Senator Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY)

“What can be done to help all of us with this financial crisis?” That was the question Patricia from North Syracuse asked me in a letter earlier this year.

A lifelong New Yorker, Patricia has faced skyrocketing grocery, heating, and gas bills that are making it increasingly difficult for her to make ends meet.

I have spent the last year talking to New Yorkers at grocery stores and gas stations across our state—from Long Island to Buffalo to the Capital Region. At every stop, I’ve heard stories just like Patricia’s.

Donald Trump promised to bring prices down “on day one.” Instead, he has unleashed cost-increasing chaos that is straining working families’ budgets across our state.

On November 3, New Yorkers get to issue a referendum on the president’s failure.

Just one week out from election day, costs are top of mind for many working Americans. Let’s talk about the cost of President Trump’s leadership and the Republican Congress that enables him.

Already, New Yorkers have paid over $6,000 more due to President Trump’s reckless policies. That $6,000 comes from rising prices on the essentials that New Yorkers rely on.

This week, the average price of gas in New York is nearly 50 percent higher than before President Trump launched his war of choice with Iran. That means every commute to work, every ride to a doctor’s appointment, every carpool to school costs about 50 percent more than it did just eight months ago.

It also means it will be more expensive for New Yorkers to heat their homes this winter. Thanks to the president’s war with Iran, the average cost of home heating oil in New York has climbed to $6.27 per gallon. That’s a 69 percent increase from this time last year. As costs continue to rise and temperatures continue to drop, some families will be forced to choose between turning on the heat and paying for other essentials like food or healthcare.

At the same time, New Yorkers are seeing higher prices at the grocery store—due to a combination of high inflation, high diesel prices due to the war with Iran, and President Trump’s tariffs. 

Amid this hardship, President Trump’s administration has played politics with our families by cutting their food assistance and ripping away their healthcare. Thanks to Trump, about 220,000 New Yorkers have already lost their SNAP benefits and 200,000 have been kicked off their healthcare.

This pain was completely avoidable. It is a result of President Trump’s backward priorities and indifference toward working families—and of the Republican Congress that refuses to rein him in.

Next week, the voters get to have their say. And while President Trump isn’t on the ballot, here’s why this election matters: Congress controls the purse strings. 

We decide whether tariffs stand, whether war is authorized, and whether heating assistance funding is renewed. But right now, Republicans in Congress are blocking us from passing meaningful legislation to check President Trump and lower costs. 

If Democrats take back the majority in November, we can change that. We can force a vote to revoke President Trump’s tariffs and refund the money Americans have paid for them. We can end the war in Iran. We can stop the corruption in Washington. And we can pass a budget that prioritizes working families.

New York is central to that fight. Competitive House seats across the state—some of which could be decided by just a few hundred votes—could determine who controls Congress. We need every New Yorker to think about what is at stake.

Patricia asked what can be done to help New Yorkers like her get their feet back under them. The answer is simple: vote for a government that is actually willing to prioritize lowering costs.

Election Day is November 3, and early voting has already begun. Make a plan to vote and bring your friends to the polls.

The cost of sitting this one out is too high.

The post ICYMI: Gillibrand Op-Ed In Empire Report: Costs Are Up. So Are The Stakes This November. appeared first on Kirsten Gillibrand | U.S. Senator for New York.

title: Gillibrand, Colleagues Demand White House Answer For Trump’s Upcoming Memecoin Event, Billed “The Most Exclusive Dinner In The World”
text:
U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY) joined eight of her Senate colleagues to push for answers from the White House on the recently announced gala dinner for top investors of the $TRUMP coin, the president’s latest scheme to continue using the office of the presidency to enrich himself.

Senator Gillibrand has long fought to stop public officials from profiting off their office. In July, she called on Congress to bar President Trump and all elected officials from issuing or sponsoring their own digital assets. This year, she also introduced the bipartisan Restore Trust in Congress Act to ban members of Congress and their families from owning or trading stocks, and the bipartisan Prediction Market Act to bar members of Congress, the president, and senior officials from trading on prediction markets.

“Public officials should not be issuing memecoins and profiting off their elected office,” said Senator Gillibrand. “Trump told Americans he would make life more affordable, but he continues to prioritize corrupt self-dealing while Americans pay higher costs for his broken promises. The time to act is now, and we must pass ethics reforms that prohibit members of Congress, the president, and their spouses from cashing in on their office.”

The upcoming November 22 event, marketed as “The Most Exclusive Dinner in the World,” invites the top 185 $TRUMP holders to a dinner and private meet and greet with the president, along with three to four undisclosed “legends.” This comes as Trump’s wealth associated with his memecoin and associated events earned him roughly $636 million in 2025 alone. Reporting also reveals that over half of Trump’s top 100 memecoin holders have utilized crypto exchanges that prohibit U.S. customer participation, indicating that many investors are based overseas and raising potential conflict of interest concerns associated with a high degree of foreign participation. 

In a letter to White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, the senators wrote, “President Trump’s continued monetization of his name and likeness once again raises serious ethical concerns, necessitating this request for a robust inquiry into the President’s financial entanglements and personal profiteering while costs for the American people continue to climb.”

“With the President poised to grow his financial holdings as a direct result of the November 22, 2026, gala dinner – particularly as American families suffer rising costs – it is incumbent upon the administration to answer to the American people about the President’s involvement in and profits from the upcoming event,” the senators continued.

The senators pressed the White House on whether the White House Counsel’s Office or a designated ethics official was consulted prior to the public announcement of President Trump’s participation in the November 22 gala dinner and VIP reception, whether there are specific guardrails in place to ensure that attendees who gain private access to the president do not use the event to solicit official executive actions, how the White House will verify that token purchases driving leaderboard rankings – including those originating from foreign wallet addresses or offshore exchanges – don’t violate the Foreign Emoluments Clause of the U.S. Constitution, and how much estimated revenue the president and his family stand to gain from trading activity leading up to November 22. 

In addition to Senator Gillibrand, the letter was signed by U.S. Senators Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-DE), Catherine Cortez Masto (D-NV), Dick Durbin (D-IL), Adam Schiff (D-CA), Elissa Slotkin (D-MI), Chris Van Hollen (D-MD), and Elizabeth Warren (D-MA).

The full text of the letter is available here.
