title: Gillibrand, Duckworth, Schiff Press FDA On Plan To Mitigate Estrogen Patch Shortage
text:
U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY) pressed the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) on its plan to mitigate the estradiol transdermal patch shortage, which is making it harder for women to manage symptoms of menopause. 

Estradiol transdermal patches are the clinically preferred, first-line treatment for managing menopause symptoms like hot flashes, night sweats, mood changes, and vaginal dryness. However, over the last year, the drug supply chain has failed to meet increased demand for estradiol patches, leaving thousands of women to navigate administrative chaos and, in some cases, ration or discontinue use of the patches.

In a letter to FDA—which was co-signed by Senators Tammy Duckworth (D-IL) and Adam Schiff (D-CA)—-Senator Gillibrand demanded additional details about how FDA is exercising its statutory authority to alleviate the estradiol patch shortage.

“Estradiol patches are a first-line, widely used, and highly effective treatment for managing menopause symptoms, and FDA should be doing everything in its power to make sure this therapy is available to all women who need it,” said Senator Gillibrand. “As the top Democrat on the Senate Aging Committee, I am demanding a clear plan from FDA to mitigate the estradiol patch shortage. This is an urgent women’s health priority, and I will not rest until we have answers.”

This letter builds on Senator Gillibrand’s work to improve menopause research, training, and care. Last month, in her capacity as ranking member of the Senate Aging Committee, Senator Gillibrand held the first ever congressional hearing on menopause. She also led a bipartisan letter to the Government Accountability Office (GAO) requesting a report on the federal government’s current role in menopause care and research. Gillibrand is also a cosponsor of the Advancing Menopause Care and Mid-Life Women’s Health Act, bipartisan legislation that would authorize $275 million over five years to strengthen and expand federal menopause research, healthcare workforce training, and education efforts related to mid-life women’s health.

The full text of the letter can be found here or below:

Dear Acting Commissioner Diamantas,

We write to express concern regarding the ongoing widespread shortage of transdermal estradiol patches. On September 16, 2026, the Senate Special Committee on Aging held a hearing highlighting the systemic menopause care gap in the United States. During the hearing, the Committee heard testimony from researchers, providers, and patients who detailed how unpredictable access to transdermal estradiol over the past year has disrupted care for hundreds of thousands of American women.

Estradiol transdermal patches represent the clinically preferred, first-line treatment for menopausal symptom management, and estrogen hormone therapy remains the single most effective intervention for severe vasomotor symptoms, including hot flashes and night sweats. The FDA’s November 2025 removal of boxed warnings on hormone replacement therapies (HRT) for menopause management was a positive step in increasing access to safe, effective care. However, this regulatory shift, coupled with increased awareness and research, surged demand for HRT among menopausal women, resulting in a dramatic year-over-year increase in prescriptions nationwide.

It has become clear that the pharmaceutical supply chain has failed to adequately respond to this surge in demand. Reports from the American Society of Health-System Pharmacists (ASHP) indicate that nearly 20 distinct estrogen patch formulations have been severely impacted by supply disruptions over the last calendar year. As a result, thousands of women are struggling to navigate administrative chaos—bouncing between competing pharmacy chains, transferring prescriptions between locations, switching formulation brands, or resorting to stretching doses or splitting patches. In some cases, patients have been forced to discontinue this effective therapy altogether.

While we acknowledge the FDA’s update on September 3, 2026 addressing the estradiol patch supply, the Committee remains concerned about the Agency’s delay in addressing this crisis and has additional questions regarding remedial steps to ensure patients can access effective therapies. Unfortunately, it took four months of inquiry for the FDA to issue basic advice telling patients to contact their pharmacist or speak with their healthcare provider. Passive monitoring and generic advice fail to adequately mitigate a nationwide manufacturing deficit.

To ensure the FDA is exercising its full statutory authority to alleviate this crisis, we request written responses to the following questions no later than November 16, 2026:

1. What criteria must the disruptions in estradiol patches meet for the FDA to declare an official estradiol patch shortage on the official Drug Shortage Database, unlocking emergency regulation tools?

2. What metrics is the FDA using to monitor manufacturer capacity for transdermal estradiol products, and when did the Agency’s staff first identify an imbalance between national demand and production volume?

3. The September 2026 update notes that the FDA is working closely with manufacturers to ensure supply of estradiol patches keeps pace with demand. What remedial steps has the FDA taken since the shortage was first identified to increase supply long-term?

 a. What is the baseline volume of production from late 2025 compared to current capacity?

 b. When do you anticipate that production will meet full market demand?

4. How many prior-approval submissions for new manufacturing lines, expanded batch sizes, site additions, specialized equipment, or other production expansion requests related to estradiol patches has the FDA received since November 2025?

 a. What is the average review time for these expedited requests?

 b. Did FDA drug shortage staff forecast market impacts following the removal of the black box warning on HRT to 
 prepare for the surge in demand?

5. Given that scaling transdermal delivery manufacturing involves complex machinery and long lead times, what interim regulatory tools is the FDA considering to address the immediate deficit?

 a. Will this involve temporary allowance of supplies from countries not previously approved for import? If so, will 
 FDA perform expedited site inspections for previously unexamined overseas manufacturing facilities?

6. Why did the FDA require four months of formal inquiry to issue basic patient guidance, and what concrete steps is the Agency taking to improve real-time public messaging and inventory reporting during active drug shortages?

7. How many staff currently work on identifying and mitigating drug shortages at FDA? How many employees are specifically focused on remedying the estradiol patch shortage?

8. What policies is the FDA implementing to check major labeling updates, boxed warning removals, or updated clinical guidelines with national supply chain forecasting to prevent similar drug shortages following updated regulatory guidance?

 a. Does the FDA’s Center for Drug Evaluation and Research (CDER) perform supply chain impact reviews prior to 
 issuing major safety labeling changes like removing boxed warnings?

Thank you for your prompt attention to this urgent women’s health priority. We look forward to receiving your response and working together to investigate this issue.

Sincerely,

###

The post Gillibrand, Duckworth, Schiff Press FDA On Plan To Mitigate Estrogen Patch Shortage appeared first on Kirsten Gillibrand | U.S. Senator for New York.

title: Gillibrand, Colleagues Slam Attorney General Blanche For Illegally Allowing Sale Of Guns To Teenagers, Increasing Likelihood Of School Shootings
text:
U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY) joined 19 of her Senate colleagues in a letter to Attorney General Todd Blanche demanding answers on the Department of Justice’s (DOJ) decision to break with decades of precedent and unilaterally refuse to enforce a prohibition against the sale of handguns to people under the age of 21. 

“The Trump administration should be doing more to keep guns out of the wrong hands – not less,” said Senator Gillibrand. “Refusing to enforce the law that bars dealers from selling handguns to teenagers makes our communities less safe and is a direct surrender to the gun lobby at the expense of American lives.” 

In their letter, the senators highlighted the enormous risks to public safety if handguns are placed in teens’ hands, writing, “The public safety implications of this decision are clear. Numerous mass shootings have been committed by perpetrators between the ages of 18 and 20, including the shooting at Robb Elementary School in Uvalde, Texas, where an 18-year-old fatally shot 19 students and two teachers and injured 18 others, as well as the shootings at a supermarket in Buffalo, New York; an Indianapolis FedEx facility and Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland, Florida. These tragic examples underscore the public safety considerations at stake and the serious risks Congress sought to address.”

“Congress enacted this prohibition as part of the Gun Control Act of 1968, clearly stating that ‘it shall be unlawful’ for an FFL to sell or transfer a handgun to a person under age 21. Nearly 60 years later, the Department’s decision to stop enforcing this provision comes not because Congress repealed or amended the law, but because the executive branch has independently concluded that these provisions are unconstitutional. This decision raises serious questions about the Department’s execution of federal law, its communications with members of the gun industry, and the implications for the enforcement of federal firearms laws nationwide,” the senators continued.

The senators concluded by requesting Blanche provide the following information on the authority and research supporting his decision: 

A detailed explanation of the legal authority on which the Department relies to stop criminal and civil enforcement of these provisions, despite their continued status as federal law;

All legal materials concerning the Department’s decision to stop enforcing 18 U.S.C. § 922(b)(1) and (c)(1) against federally licensed firearm dealers that sell handguns to individuals between the ages of 18 and 20;

Any analysis conducted or reviewed by the Department regarding the potential public-safety consequences of changing federal enforcement policy for handgun sales to individuals between the ages of 18 and 20; and

A list of all investigations, prosecutions, and civil or criminal enforcement actions affected by the Department’s decision, including any matters declined, suspended, dismissed, or otherwise modified, and the reasons for each action.

In addition to Senator Gillibrand, the letter was signed by U.S. Senators Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-DE), Cory Booker (D-NJ), Chris Coons (D-DE), Dick Durbin (D-IL), Mazie Hirono (D-HI), Tim Kaine (D-VA), Mark Kelly (D-AZ), Andy Kim (D-NJ), Amy Klobuchar (D-MN), Ed Markey (D-MA), Chris Murphy (D-CT), Alex Padilla (D-CA), Jack Reed (D-RI), Adam Schiff (D-CA), Chuck Schumer (D-NY), Elizabeth Warren (D-MA), Peter Welch (D-VT), and Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI).

Senator Gillibrand has long fought for commonsense gun safety laws. She wrote the interstate gun trafficking ban that became law as part of the Bipartisan Safer Communities Act, which has helped take over 6,000 guns off the streets. When the Trump administration stopped providing updates on prosecutions under the ban, Gillibrand successfully demanded that DOJ restore transparency and resume the updates. She also introduced the Age 21 Act to raise the minimum age to buy assault weapons to 21. In July, she called out the Trump administration’s dangerous rollbacks of gun safety regulations, like those that hold lawbreaking gun dealers accountable and keep guns away from people with serious mental illness.

The full text of the letter is available below. A copy of the letter is available here. 

Dear Attorney General Blanche:

We write regarding the U.S. Department of Justice’s (the Department) decision to cease enforcement of longstanding federal restrictions on the sale of handguns to individuals under the age of 21 by federally licensed firearms dealers (FFLs). This significant change in federal enforcement policy raises serious questions about the Department’s legal justification, and we request information regarding the analysis underlying its decision.

On September 18, 2026, the Department’s Office of Legal Counsel (OLC) published a legal opinion concluding that 18 U.S.C. § 922(b)(1) and (c)(1)—the federal prohibition on FFLs selling handguns to 18- to 20-year-olds—violate the Second Amendment, and that federal prosecutors may no longer prosecute FFLs that sell handguns to 18- to 20-year-olds who are not otherwise prohibited from gun possession.[1] Congress enacted this prohibition as part of the Gun Control Act of 1968, clearly stating that “it shall be unlawful” for an FFL to sell or transfer a handgun to a person under age 21.[2] Nearly 60 years later, the Department’s decision to stop enforcing this provision comes not because Congress repealed or amended the law, but because the Executive Branch has independently concluded that these provisions are unconstitutional. This decision raises serious questions about the Department’s execution of federal law, its communications with members of the gun industry, and the implications for the enforcement of federal firearms laws nationwide.

The Department’s OLC opinion acknowledges the constitutionality of age-based firearms restrictions has “deeply divided members of the federal bench.” Given the ongoing nature of this legal dispute, the Department’s decision that it may cease enforcement of federal law by executive fiat, rather than continue defending and enforcing the statute, represents an expansive and concerning assertion of executive authority.

The public safety implications of this decision are clear. Numerous mass shootings have been committed by perpetrators between the ages of 18 and 20, including the shooting at Robb Elementary School in Uvalde, Texas, where an 18-year-old fatally shot 19 students and two teachers and injured 18 others, as well as the shootings at a supermarket in Buffalo, New York; an Indianapolis FedEx facility and Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland, Florida. These tragic examples underscore the public safety considerations at stake and the serious risks Congress sought to address. The Department’s decision to unilaterally cease enforcement of this provision of law raises serious questions and concerns. Thus, we request the Department provide:

 A detailed explanation of the legal authority on which the Department relies to stop criminal and civil enforcement of these provisions, despite their continued status as federal law;

All legal materials concerning the Department’s decision to stop enforcing 18 U.S.C. § 922(b)(1) and (c)(1) against federally licensed firearm dealers that sell handguns to individuals between the ages of 18 and 20;

Any analysis conducted or reviewed by the Department regarding the potential public-safety consequences of changing federal enforcement policy for handgun sales to individuals between the ages of 18 and 20; and

A list of all investigations, prosecutions, and civil or criminal enforcement actions affected by the Department’s decision, including any matters declined, suspended, dismissed, or otherwise modified, and the reasons for each action.

Please provide the requested information and documents by November 16, 2026.

###

title: Gillibrand, Colleagues Demand Trump FCC Withdraw Proposal To Undermine E-Rate Program
text:
Lawmakers Argue That Dismantling E-Rate Will Widen The Digital Divide And Raise Costs For The Communities That Can Least Afford It

U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY) joined a bicameral group of colleagues in urging Federal Communications Commission (FCC) Chairman Brendan Carr to withdraw the Commission’s damaging proposal to eliminate or limit the E-Rate program. In June, the Carr FCC voted to open a rulemaking examining E-Rate, which helps schools and libraries across the country afford reliable internet access.

“Every school should have the resources it needs to provide our kids with a high-quality education,” said Senator Gillibrand. “Millions of children who lack reliable internet access are at risk of falling behind without the critical connectivity that the E-Rate program provides. I urge the FCC to immediately withdraw its harmful proposal, and I will continue fighting to protect E-Rate and keep investing in our schools, libraries, and future leaders.”

E-Rate helps over 96% of U.S. public schools access high-speed internet. In 2025, nearly $182 million in E-Rate funding was committed to school districts and libraries across New York State, helping them afford reliable internet. 

On Long Island, E-Rate saved Suffolk County public libraries over $300,000 last year, covering roughly 60% of their broadband bills. At the same time, internet demand in Nassau County school districts jumped 31% over the past year, a spike that could put significant strain on district budgets without E-Rate discounts.

In the letter, the lawmakers wrote, “Schools and libraries help develop the next generation of engineers, scientists, and cybersecurity professionals, including in communities that have historically lacked access to those opportunities. Cutting E-Rate would narrow that talent pipeline. Maintaining connectivity in every school and library is therefore an investment in America’s technological leadership, economic competitiveness, and national security.”

“We strongly support measures to protect children online and address concerns around excessive screen time. But cutting E-Rate is not a child-safety measure. E-Rate funds broadband connectivity — not laptops, tablets, applications, or online content — and recipients must already comply with the Children’s Internet Protection Act, including by using filtering and blocking tools, adopting internet-safety policies, and educating students about appropriate online behavior. States and local communities, meanwhile, are developing targeted policies governing when and how students use devices in schools — an appropriate way to address screen-time concerns, rather than cutting broadband support. The Commission should not use child safety as a pretext to dismantle the secure, managed broadband infrastructure that schools and libraries need to educate students and help them navigate the digital world safely,” the lawmakers continued.

In addition to Senator Gillibrand, the letter was signed by U.S. Senators Angela Alsobrooks (D-MD), Tammy Baldwin (D-WI), Michael Bennet (D-CO), Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-DE), Cory Booker (D-NJ), Maria Cantwell (D-WA), Chris Coons (D-DE), Catherine Cortez Masto (D-NV), Tammy Duckworth (D-IL), Dick Durbin (D-IL), John Fetterman (D-PA), Ruben Gallego (D-AZ), Maggie Hassan (D-NH), Martin Heinrich (D-NM), John Hickenlooper (D-CO), Mazie Hirono (D-HI), Tim Kaine (D-VA), Mark Kelly (D-AZ), Andy Kim (D-NJ), Angus King (I-ME), Amy Klobuchar (D-MN), Ben Ray Luján (D-NM), Edward Markey (D-MA), Jeff Merkley (D-OR), Chris Murphy (D-CT), Patty Murray (D-WA), Alex Padilla (D-CA), Gary Peters (D-MI), Jack Reed (D-RI), Jacky Rosen (D-NV), Bernie Sanders (I-VT), Brian Schatz (D-HI), Adam Schiff (D-CA), Chuck Schumer (D-NY), Jeanne Shaheen (D-NH), Elissa Slotkin (D-MI), Tina Smith (D-MN), Chris Van Hollen (D-MD), Mark Warner (D-VA), Raphael Warnock (D-GA), Elizabeth Warren (D-MA), Peter Welch (D-VT), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), and Ron Wyden (D-OR).

It was also signed by U.S. Representatives Doris Matsui (CA-07), Rob Menendez (NJ-08), Grace Meng (NY-06), and more than 60 other members of the House Democratic Caucus.

Senator Gillibrand has long fought to hold the FCC accountable and expand internet access for students across New York. During the COVID-19 pandemic, she urged the FCC to immediately provide more E-Rate funding so students learning remotely could access reliable internet from home. She also demanded answers from the FCC about its decision to block states that had already invested in rural broadband from a new federal funding program for unserved communities. Last year, she led the New York delegation in pushing the Trump administration to protect more than $270 million in federal broadband funding that New York can use to make internet service more affordable.

The full text of the letter is available HERE.

title: New Study: Families In New York Have Had To Spend $6,000+ More Under Trump
text:
JEC Report: The Average Household In New York Has Had To Pay An Additional $6,000+ For Goods And Services Due To Rising Costs Under President Trump

This week, a new Joint Economic Committee (JEC) – Minority report found that as of September 2026, the average household in New York has had to pay an additional $6,000+ for goods and services due to rising costs under President Trump. When campaigning in 2024, candidate Trump promised, “Starting on day one of my new administration, we will end inflation, and we will make America affordable again.” 

In response to the new report and Republicans’ broken promises, U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand issued the following statement:

“President Trump and congressional Republicans promised to lower costs and end inflation. Instead, they’ve made life $6,000 more expensive for New Yorkers,” said Senator Gillibrand. “Look at what they have done: they gutted Medicaid and cut Medicare and healthcare subsidies to fund tax breaks for billionaires, launched a war that increased gas prices, and supported tariffs to make groceries and essentials more expensive. I will not stop fighting to lower New Yorkers’ costs and hold this administration accountable for hurting working families and small businesses across our state.” 

The new report follows JEC’s September study that found that President Trump’s vanity projects – including construction of the new White House ballroom and the no-bid contract to paint the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, among others – are expected to cost more than $1.8 billion, highlighting the administration’s egregiously misplaced priorities and lack of interest in spending money to lower costs and help the American people.

Additional breakdowns of the JEC report:

Housing Costs

New York families have had to spend an additional $1,310 on housing costs such as rent and mortgage payments since President Trump took office.

Grocery Costs

Americans paid $310 more for groceries in President Trump’s first year than in 2024, and grocery prices are now more than 4 percent higher than when Trump took office.

Beef and coffee prices are hitting Americans especially hard. Since the president took office, the average price of ground beef has risen almost every month to a record high of more than $7 per pound. Coffee prices also spiked and are now more than $9 per pound.

Energy Costs

Gas prices have soared since the start of Trump’s Iran war. In total, people across New York have spent an additional $4 billion on gas since the beginning of the war. That has cost the average family in New York an additional $739 in gas costs.

Families in New York spent $190 more on electricity in 2025 under President Trump than they did in 2024. And, in just the first seven months of 2026, they spent $258 more on electricity than they did in the first seven months of 2024.

Home heating oil prices in New York are at record highs, which means it will now cost a family $1,558 to fill their heating oil tank, $598 more than at this time last year. If prices stay this high, then New York families will have to pay a total of $2,504 to heat their homes this winter, a 32 percent increase compared to last winter.

Health Care Costs

Because of Trump and Republicans’ refusal to extend the Affordable Care Act (ACA) tax cuts that help people afford their health insurance, monthly premiums for ACA plans rose over 50 percent on average in 2026 compared to last year. Meanwhile, deductibles surged to record highs, increasing by more than $1,000 on average.

Sources: Bureau of Labor Statistics Consumer Price Index and Average Price Data, Census Bureau’s American Community Survey, Joint Economic Committee – Republicans, Bureau of Economic Analysis, U.S. Department of Agriculture, Walmart.com, AAA.com, Federal Highway Administration, Energy Information Administration, Kaiser Family Foundation. Gas cost calculations are current through October 14, 2026, heating oil as of October 5th.

###

title: ICYMI: Gillibrand Op-Ed In The Hill: The System Failed Jane Doe. Congress Can Fix It.
text:
In case you missed it, U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand published an opinion piece in The Hill demanding that Congress take action to support victims of sexual assault in the wake of allegations of a horrific gang rape at Cornell University.

Senator Gillibrand argues that Congress—after spending two weeks debating regulations for college sports—must find time to protect students on college campuses. She urges passage of her bipartisan legislation, the Campus Accountability and Safety Act (CASA), and describes how that legislation could have helped Jane Doe and stands to help other survivors in the future if passed.

The full text of the op-ed can be found here or below:

The System Failed Jane Doe. Congress Can Fix It.

By Senator Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY)

In recent weeks, the horrific allegations of sexual assault at a Cornell University fraternity house have sparked public outrage.

But as debates about campus culture and law enforcement lapses permeated the public conscience, Congress made clear that it had a very different priority: debating regulations for college sports. Not a second was spent on campus safety at a time that one in four undergraduate women report being sexually assaulted at school. At Cornell, that figure is more than one in three.

There is no question: the system has failed Jane Doe.

This is not just a problem with one case, one fraternity, or one university. Jane Doe’s story echoes a heartbreaking reality on campuses across the country. Time and time again, victims experience the same story: they report, then watch their perpetrators get by with a slap on the wrist.

In 2016, America watched Stanford swimmer Brock Turner serve just three months in jail for raping an unconscious woman behind a campus dumpster. The survivor’s victim impact statement went viral. Over a million people signed petitions calling for the judge in Turner’s case to be removed. Lawmakers changed the state’s sentencing laws.

This should have been a turning point. It wasn’t.

In 2016, Baylor also came under fire after an investigation found administrators had discouraged students from reporting sexual assault. In 2021, USC announced it would pay millions to women who said the university ignored years of complaints about sexual abuse by its campus gynecologist. In the years since, dozens of institutions have come under federal investigation over alleged mishandling of Title IX sexual violence cases.

A system that fails survivors again and again is fundamentally broken. The price of a college education shouldn’t include a 25+% chance of being sexually assaulted.

Congress must do more to protect students.

We must pass the Campus Accountability and Safety Act (CASA). 

CASA is commonsense, bipartisan legislation. It would hold institutions accountable, uphold a fair process for students, and give sexual assault survivors a trauma-informed advocate to help them through the adjudication process.

Cornell offers confidential resources for students, and we don’t know the extent to which Jane Doe knew about or used them. But not all universities offer those resources, and even if they do, many students don’t know they exist.

That’s how CASA could help. 

First, it would require a trained, confidential advocate to be available to survivors of sexual assault on every campus.

The trauma of sexual assault can impair memory and make bureaucracy feel impossible. Having an advocate who is trained in trauma-informed care ensures that survivors are not re-traumatized by the very system meant to protect them.

Such an advocate could have been life-changing for someone like Jane Doe.

They could have walked Doe through the complex disciplinary process that comes with reporting an assault. They could have talked her through her options, including the difference between Cornell’s disciplinary process and the criminal process. And when Doe chose to report, they could have acted as her liaison with the university and law enforcement, sparing her the trauma of reliving her experience every time she spoke with a different authority figure. 

Crucially, CASA would require campus staff who receive reports of sexual assault and domestic violence – including the Cornell Health medical clinic employee Jane Doe saw – to provide those students with contact information for the on-campus advocate and an explanation of the services they offer. 

Second, CASA would require uniform, rigorous training for all campus personnel involved in investigating and adjudicating sexual assault cases. 

That training could have helped prevent critical errors in Doe’s case.

For example, Doe’s lawyer alleges that the Tompkins County District Attorney (DA) never contacted her after she made her initial statement to Cornell police. A New York Times investigation later showed that a key statement from Doe’s testimony—“I can say with 100 percent confidence I was raped”—was left out of the six-page statement that was sent to the DA. 

Better-trained investigators are far less likely to make that mistake. 

At the same time, a CASA advocate could have helped Doe review her testimony and caught the omission. Then, once the complaint was submitted to the DA, they could have helped follow up on her case and demanded that her complaint be taken seriously.

Advocates and training help survivors navigate the system—but that is only half the battle. CASA also fixes the system itself, making it more transparent and fair for all students.

The legislation would mandate a uniform process for conducting campus disciplinary proceedings surrounding sexual assault. 

That means no separate track for athletes or students in fraternities.

CASA also protects students who come forward by encouraging the adoption of a practical amnesty policy in cases like Jane Doe’s where alcohol or drugs are involved. CASA would help shield students who report in good faith from campus disciplinary actions for drinking or illegal substance use. 

And finally, CASA would require colleges and universities to disclose key data about the prevalence of sexual assault on their campuses and the outcomes of sexual assault investigations. Institutions that fail to comply would face financial penalties.

Transparency creates accountability. If students and families can see what is happening on campus, and how universities respond, institutions will finally be incentivized to put safety first.

Passing CASA will not end sexual violence on college campuses, nor will it undo the harm already inflicted on countless survivors. Changing the culture that allows campus sexual assault to persist will require sustained commitment at every level—from universities, students, families, law enforcement, and lawmakers. But establishing a fair process, giving survivors an advocate, and mandating real accountability is an essential start.

The system failed Jane Doe. It has failed too many survivors for too long. Congress can change that. We must pass the Campus Accountability and Safety Act.

title: Gillibrand, Schumer, Torres Urge Acceleration Of Federal Lithium-Ion Battery Regulation Amidst E-Bike Fatalities
text:
Import of Faulty Lithium-Ion Battery Powered Micromobility Products Linked to Nationwide Deaths

Today, U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY), along with Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY) and Congressman Ritchie Torres (D-NY), called on Peter Feldman, Acting Chair of the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC), to complete the rulemaking process to set a mandatory federal standard for lithium-ion batteries in micromobility products such as e-bikes and e-scooters. In their letter, the members underscored the concerning number of lithium-ion battery-related fatalities among micromobility products across the country, particularly in New York City.

They wrote, “To prevent further destruction to our communities and protect lives, we urge the Consumer Product Safety Commission…to immediately work through stakeholder comments and swiftly complete the rulemaking process for the proposed rule, ‘Safety Standard for Lithium-Ion Batteries Used in Micromobility Products and Electrical Systems of Micromobility Products Containing Such Batteries.’” 

The members cited the CPSC staff’s pre-existing awareness of the dangers of these batteries, as a 2026 CPSC report acknowledged 367 lithium-ion battery-related fires resulting in 45 fatalities from 2017 through 2024 among all micromobility products. While this has become an issue all across the nation, the numbers are especially concerning in New York City. The members wrote that just this year, the Fire Department of the City of New York reported 362 fires and 5 deaths among users of e‑bikes, e-scooters, and similar single‑person devices.

Local communities have attempted to implement safety measures, from setting standards for retailers to banning the use of micromobility products in certain locations. However, the members emphasized the necessity of action on the federal level. They maintained, “While these rules attempt to achieve safety, the only way to effectively prevent future fires is by setting mandatory federal standards for lithium-ion batteries. […] By finalizing this rule and setting standards for these batteries, the Commission can ensure that cheap and defective batteries do not enter the U.S. market.”

Senator Gillibrand has long championed a push toward the enforcement of e-bike safety standards on the federal level. She is the lead Senate sponsor of the Setting Consumer Standards for Lithium-Ion Batteries Act, which passed the House of Representatives on April 28, 2025 and awaits passage in the Senate.

title: Gillibrand Calls For Legislation To Improve Social Security Benefits Following Announcement Of 2027 COLA
text:
80% of Social Security Recipients Say Similar COLA Would Not Adequately Compensate For Rising Cost Of Living

Washington, D.C. — Today, U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY) called for passage of her legislation to strengthen Social Security benefits following the release of the 2027 cost-of-living adjustment (COLA). The Social Security Administration (SSA) announced this morning that Social Security benefits will increase by 3.6% in 2027.

“Our seniors have spent a lifetime of hard work paying into Social Security, but their checks simply aren’t keeping up with rising costs,” said Senator Gillibrand. “This year’s cost-of-living adjustment is not enough to make up for skyrocketing costs for groceries, gas, heating, and healthcare in President Trump’s America. As the top Democrat on the Senate Aging Committee, I’m fighting to pass the Boosting Benefits and COLAs for Seniors Act to protect and expand Social Security benefits long-term by changing the formula used to calculate COLAs to better account for the expenses that seniors face.”

The 3.6% COLA comes as rising costs are making it harder for American seniors to make ends meet. Already, New Yorkers have paid over $5,500 more due to President Trump’s reckless policies. In September alone, inflation rose to 3.7%.

The 2027 COLA will amount to an increase of about $75 per month. 80 percent of current Social Security recipients say a similar increase would not adequately compensate for the rising cost of living.

Senator Gillibrand’s Boosting Benefits and COLAs for Seniors Act—which was introduced last year—would direct SSA to adjust benefits based on the Consumer Price Index for Americans aged 62 or older (CPI-E), rather than the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners (CPI-W). The CPI-E more accurately accounts for the actual costs incurred by older Americans, such as medical expenses and prescription drug costs—making it a more reflective index to use when calculating benefits.

Additionally, this week, Senator Gillibrand sent a letter to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics urging the administration to improve data collection for the CPI-E. This letter follows the Trump administration’s attempt to cut funding to the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) in Fiscal Year 2027, as well as reports that staffing cuts at BLS have already eroded the reliability of economic data.

The text of the Boosting Benefits and COLAs for Seniors Act can be found here. Senator Gillibrand’s letter to the Bureau of Labor Statistics can be found here.

In addition to the Boosting Benefits and COLAs for Seniors Act, Senator Gillibrand has proposed multiple pieces of legislation to help ensure that seniors can continue to get the full benefits they are owed and to reverse disastrous Trump administration cuts to SSA:

The Social Security Expansion Act would extend the solvency of Social Security for 75 years by requiring the wealthiest American households to pay their fair share of payroll taxes. Under the current formula, a CEO making $20 million a year pays the same amount into Social Security as individuals making $184,500 a year. This legislation would lift the cap on Social Security, requiring income above $250,000 to be subject to the Social Security payroll tax and thus increasing the amount paid into the Social Security trust fund to increase its longevity.

The Keep Billionaires Out of Social Security Act would reverse Trump administration cuts to SSA, prohibit unnecessary Social Security field office closures, boost staffing levels to help reduce wait times and make it easier for seniors and people with disabilities to get help over the phone, protect Americans’ data, and provide the resources SSA needs to help approve earned benefits quickly.

title: Gillibrand, Colleagues File Amicus Brief In Lawsuit Against Trump’s Department Of Housing And Urban Development For Attacking Fair Housing Program
text:
U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY), ranking member of the Senate Appropriations Transportation, Housing and Urban Development (THUD) Subcommittee, joined 20 of her Senate colleagues in submitting an amicus brief supporting a federal judge’s ruling that the Trump administration’s Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) unlawfully restricted funding to groups that investigate and enforce laws against housing discrimination. The amicus brief argues that HUD’s unprecedented attempt to direct $46 million away from fair housing organizations – while diverting an additional $10 million to government agencies with separate appropriations – has no lawful justification and would harm the nation’s fair housing enforcement infrastructure.

“Fair housing organizations work every day to protect New Yorkers from discrimination when they rent or buy a home,” said Senator Gillibrand. “Without the federal funding Congress appropriated, these groups could be forced to shut their doors, allowing housing discrimination to go unchecked and leaving families with nowhere to turn. I am proud to join this amicus brief and will keep fighting to make sure the Trump administration follows the law and delivers the funds as Congress intended.”

The senators began the brief, “Congress intended [the Fair Housing Initiatives Program (FHIP)] to foster a nationwide network of private organizations, like Plaintiffs, that can aid the federal government in uncovering and eliminating housing discrimination. Since Congress piloted FHIP in 1988 and codified it in 1992, FHIP has consistently sustained private fair housing organizations through three grant streams: the Private Enforcement Initiative (‘PEI’) to support investigative and enforcement activities; the Education and Outreach Initiative (‘EOI’); and the Fair Housing Organization Initiative (‘FHOI’) to build organizational capacity. With this funding, private organizations handle most housing discrimination complaints and enforcement nationwide.”

“HUD’s July 2, 2026 Notices of Funding Opportunity (‘NOFOs’) endanger fair housing organizations and their vital work. The NOFOs deviate from FHIP’s authorizing statute, decades of FHIP practice, and Congress’s intent. For the first time since FHIP’s codification in 1992, the FY2025 NOFOs provide no new awards for PEI or EOI—the lifeblood of fair housing organizations—nor do they fulfill existing multi-year PEI awards. Instead, HUD attempts to direct $46 million—the vast majority of funds—away from existing qualified organizations in favor of organizations with no experience in fair housing enforcement, while diverting the remaining $10 million to governmental agencies for which Congress separately appropriated. These unprecedented actions have no lawful justification and would seriously harm the nation’s fair housing enforcement infrastructure. The district court rightly vacated HUD’s unlawful notices and directed funding to flow under the prior framework. HUD’s request to stay that well-founded order should be denied,” the senators argued.

The senators concluded, “The Doles Memo’s stated aims are misleading and contrary to FHIP’s purposes as well. It claims the FY2025 NOFOs will ‘expand geographic coverage,’ ‘broaden’ expertise, and ‘strengthen the long-term resilience of the national fair housing infrastructure.’ HUD’s NOFOs do the opposite—losing geographic coverage, expertise, and organizational resilience by concentrating FHIP funding in a handful of grants that existing organizations cannot receive. Worse, the Doles Memo treats fair housing organizations like maligned welfare recipients—charging them with ‘perpetual dependence’ on federal funding. FHIP’s goal always has been to sustain these organizations as a vital organ of the fair housing enforcement system, particularly in areas underserved without federal resources. HUD’s NOFOs, if unaddressed, would set fair housing enforcement back decades. Defendants’ Motion for Stay should be denied.”

The brief was submitted to the United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit in the case of Massachusetts Fair Housing Center; National Fair Housing Alliance v. Department of Housing and Urban Development. Senator Gillibrand was joined by Senators Chris Van Hollen (D-MD), Cory Booker (D-NJ), Patty Murray (D-WA), Jack Reed (D-RI), Chuck Schumer (D-NY), Mark Warner (D-VA), Jeff Merkley (D-OR), Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), Brian Schatz (D-HI), Tim Kaine (D-VA), Elizabeth Warren (D-MA), Edward Markey (D-MA), Catherine Cortez Masto (D-NV), Tina Smith (D-MN), Raphael Warnock (D-GA), Peter Welch (D-VT), Andy Kim (D-NJ), Ruben Gallego (D-AZ), Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-DE), and Angela Alsobrooks (D-MD).

Senator Gillibrand has repeatedly held the Trump administration and HUD accountable for their failures on fair housing: 

In August, she wrote to HUD urging the Trump administration to immediately rescind the FY25 and FY26 Notices of Funding Opportunity for the Fair Housing Initiatives Program (FHIP), which are the subject of this court case, and instead re-issue NOFOs consistent with the law and congressional intent. 

Earlier this year, she secured $86 million for fair housing programs, including $56 million for FHIP, when negotiating the Fiscal Year 2026 funding bill to support the critical work fair housing organizations do in New York and across the country. The Trump administration proposed eliminating FHIP entirely. 

Last year, she called out HUD for its failures to enforce our nation’s fair housing laws – a letter HUD has still not responded to nearly one year later.

Last year, she led Senate Democrats in pushing HUD to halt plans to overhaul a key homelessness program, which could have forced nearly 200,000 people back onto the streets. In May, she called out HUD Secretary Scott Turner over his failure to show measurable progress on housing affordability and to release HUD’s long-overdue report on homelessness data. Two weeks later, the administration released the report.

Full text of the argument in the brief can be viewed here.

title: Gillibrand, Colleagues Reintroduce Legislation To Increase Access To Life-Saving Breast And Gynecological Cancer Screenings
text:
U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY) joined Senator Patty Murray (D-WA) in reintroducing the Jeanette Acosta Invest in Women’s Health Act, legislation that would increase the availability of life-saving cancer screenings at safety net healthcare providers like Planned Parenthood. The bill would create new grant and pilot programs to expand access to preventive services and screenings for breast and gynecological cancers—especially for low-income women and women of color—and train healthcare providers in providing high-quality cancer screening, early detection, and follow-up care.

The legislation is named for Jeanette Acosta, who was a fierce women’s health advocate, former congressional staffer, and White House intern in the Obama administration. In 2017, she lost her battle with cervical cancer at the age of 32.

“Millions of women in the U.S. do not have access to preventative screenings that could catch deadly illnesses early and save their lives. That is a national tragedy that demands action,” said Senator Gillibrand. “The Jeanette Acosta Invest in Women’s Health Act is a commonsense piece of legislation to increase access to life-saving breast and gynecological cancer screenings for women who may otherwise slip through the cracks. I am doing everything I can to get this bill across the finish line.”

“It is an honor that the Jeanette Acosta Invest in Women’s Health Act of 2026 is in our daughter’s name. Over eight years ago cervical cancer took the life of our precious and valiant daughter, Jeanette. At the young age of 32, after one year of battling her cancer and suffering incomparable pain and extensive treatment, Jeanette died from her advanced cancer. Jeanette prayed that women be spared from the agony of cervical cancer, and this bill would help to achieve her hope for many women,” said Frank X. Acosta, Ph.D., Jeanette Acosta’s father. “This bill will have a lasting and positive national impact in the fight against cancers that afflict women. During her own fight with cancer, Jeanette reached out and provided support and encouragement to other women coping with cancer. She also emphasized the importance of prevention against the onset of cervical cancer. Jeanette, always a warrior for social justice, wanted to shine a light on the disparities to access to prevention and cancer health services for low-income, Latina, and Black women. This bill would brightly illuminate and help to close the gap between cancer prevention and health services and the countless women who have not and may not be able to access these services. Jeanette would adamantly support this bill.”

“I’m proud to reintroduce the Jeanette Acosta Invest in Women’s Health Act in honor of Jeanette Acosta, a fierce advocate who fought to make sure every woman could get the health care she needs,” said Senator Murray. “Too many women suffer preventable deaths because they didn’t have access to the cancer screenings that would have detected their condition early on. That is an unacceptable tragedy. We know that early detection saves lives—not to mention health care costs—and investing in preventive services to help more women get treatment before it’s too late is just common sense. I’m not going to stop fighting to pass this crucial piece of legislation in Jeanette’s memory.”

In addition to Senators Gillibrand and Murray, the Jeanette Acosta Invest in Women’s Health Act is cosponsored by Senators Angela Alsobrooks (D-MD), Tammy Baldwin (D-WI), Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), Cory Booker (D-NJ), Tammy Duckworth (D-IL), Ruben Gallego (D-AZ), Amy Klobuchar (D-MN), Jeff Merkley (D-OR), Jacky Rosen (D-NV), Adam Schiff (D-CA), Jeanne Shaheen (D-NH), Chris Van Hollen (D-MD), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), and Ron Wyden (D-OR).

The bill is endorsed by: American College of Obstetrics and Gynecology, American Society for Reproductive Medicine, Black Women’s Health Imperative, Human Rights Watch, In Our Own Voice: National Black Women’s Reproductive Justice Agenda, National Asian Pacific American Women’s Forum, National Council of Jewish Women, National Family Planning & Reproductive Health Association, National Latina Institute for Reproductive Justice, National Partnership for Women & Families, National Women’s Law Center Action Fund, Ovarian Cancer Research Alliance, and Planned Parenthood Federation of America.

Senator Gillibrand has long been a champion for women’s health. Last month, she held the first ever congressional hearing on menopause, shedding light on the need for additional federal support for menopause research, training, and care. Gillibrand also leads the Moms Matter Act—part of the Momnibus Act that was reintroduced earlier this year—which would increase investments in maternal mental health programs and expand this vital workforce to better support moms and pregnant women. She also leads the Healthy Maternity and Obstetric Medicine (MOM) Act, legislation designed to expand healthcare access for pregnant women and ensure they receive coverage that meets their needs.

The full text of the Jeanette Acosta Invest in Women’s Health Act can be found here.

title: Gillibrand, Colleagues Introduce Bicameral Legislation To Depoliticize Military Promotions
text:
U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY), a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, joined a bicameral group of colleagues to introduce the Military Officer Promotion Integrity Act. This bill would protect qualified military officers from being arbitrarily removed from promotion consideration for ideological or political reasons by establishing clear standards, basic due process, and meaningful independent review.

“Officers who have earned a promotion deserve to be judged on their qualifications and nothing else,” said Senator Gillibrand. “Secretary Hegseth has pushed out our best and brightest, cutting some of the most highly trained, most qualified people in our armed services and leaving our military rudderless. I will keep fighting to curb Secretary Hegseth’s ability to jeopardize our national security and military preparedness and ensure our military is led by qualified officers capable of keeping Americans safe.”

Defense Secretary Hegseth has repeatedly blocked women and minority officers from promotions and criticized diversity initiatives in the military. The new legislation reins in Secretary Hegseth’s inconsistent and politicized leadership and mandates that an officer can only be removed from promotion recommendations based on the following criteria:

The officer engaged in misconduct;

Newly discovered, material adverse information unavailable to the promotion selection board materially affects the qualifications of the officer for promotion;

The officer no longer satisfies statutory qualifications for promotion; or

Removal is required for reasons of national security or military necessity

Senator Gillibrand has been a leading voice in holding Secretary Hegseth accountable for his reckless leadership of the Department of Defense. During his confirmation hearing, she challenged his previous denigration of women in the military and has repeatedly called for his resignation, most recently after eight sailors in the USS Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group attempted suicide. In April, after reports that Hegseth blocked or delayed promotions for more than a dozen Black and female senior officers, she called for a Senate Armed Services Committee hearing on the matter. 

In addition to Senator Gillibrand, the legislation is cosponsored in the Senate by U.S. Senators Richard Blumenthal (D-CT), Jeanne Shaheen (D-NH), Jacky Rosen (D-NV), and Mazie K. Hirono (D-HI). It is cosponsored in the House by U.S. Representatives Chrissy Houlahan (D-PA-06) and Marilyn Strickland (D-WA-10).

The bill is endorsed by VoteVets, Protect Democracy, the National Women’s Law Center (NWLC), and Retired Major General Steve Lepper, co-founder of the Former JAG Working Group.

text:

Footage of Senator Gillibrand’s interview with Pamela Brown can be found here.

Transcripts of key moments can be found below:

ON HEGSETH’S INABILITY TO STAND UP TO PRESIDENT TRUMP AND ENSURE OUR MILITARY KEEPS AMERICANS SAFE:

He’s firing people not based on qualifications, but how they look, the color of their skin. These are all red flags that this is a secretary of defense who does not know how to lead our country productively to keep Americans safer.

ON THE TRUMP ADMINISTRATION’S LACK OF LEADERSHIP THAT FORCED SERVICE MEMBERS IN THE USS LINCOLN STRIKE GROUP TO SERVE IN DISMAL CONDITIONS:

BROWN: You’re also calling for congressional hearings after the Navy confirmed to you in a letter that eight sailors on the USS Abraham Lincoln fleet – we should note there you have the carrier and then you have the fleet – that there were attempted suicides. So, what more have you learned about the conditions on board? Not just the carrier itself, which I was an embed on for three days back in July, but also just the other warships around it, where there were attempted suicides as well.

GILLIBRAND: Well, this goes to the lack of leadership of Secretary Hegseth again, and ultimately President Trump, deploying our service members for months upon months, far longer than they expected, not giving them the dwell time, the time at home that they need to recuperate and be ready to continue to go back into combat over and over again. We wrote a letter asking what is the status and well-being of the service members that are deployed, and the answer we got was shocking. Eight people have attempted suicide on these warships. Two threw themselves overboard, which, according to experts, is the most extreme scenario you can imagine being a sailor on a warship. And so I have serious questions about how Secretary Hegseth is leading this military and, ultimately, President Trump.

ON THE SERIOUS AND HORRIFIC ALLEGATIONS IN THE CORNELL RAPE CASE AND THE NEED FOR LEGISLATION LIKE THE CAMPUS ACCOUNTABILITY AND SAFETY ACT TO SUPPORT SURVIVORS: 

BROWN: I want to turn to another issue, and that is this Cornell rape civil suit that is getting a lot of attention. You have called the allegations “serious and horrific.” You and Republican Senator Chuck Grassley have introduced legislation to combat sexual assault on college campuses, but that bill was never passed. What role can Congress play here?

GILLIBRAND: Well, we should pass our legislation immediately. What it does is create rules of the road so that every student is protected on campus. We have to make sure that there’s a person who’s highly trained to receive these allegations in the first instance to tell a survivor what his or her rights are, what opportunity she has to report either through a civilian system, through a college system, or through a criminal system. She or he is given just the basic tools of advocacy about what’s going to happen to their lives and whether the school will provide accommodations. And then you need a process that is a highly informed process, that is legitimate, and doesn’t pit one student against another unfairly in a circumstance that doesn’t actually resolve to justice. And so we need reform on all of these college campuses. It’s not right that kids go off to school and are not safe. It’s not right that what happened in this instance doesn’t appear to have been assessed properly. So I’m grateful that the DA is looking at it again.

title: Gillibrand Introduces Bill To Protect Americans’ Data From Big Tech And AI Companies
text:
Today, U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY) reintroduced the Data Protection Act. This legislation would create a new independent federal agency to protect Americans’ data, ensure fair data practices, and help the government adapt to rapidly evolving digital technologies.

“As AI continues to evolve, it is more important than ever that we take action to crack down on tech companies that misuse Americans’ data,” said Senator Gillibrand. “Currently, Big Tech companies are free to sell individuals’ data to the highest bidder without fear of real consequences, posing a severe threat to privacy and civil rights. My bill would create an independent federal agency to protect data and privacy, equipped with the resources to give Americans the meaningful protection they deserve.”

Data privacy is a growing concern in the United States. In 2025 alone, more than 3,300 data breaches exposed over 278 million individuals’ personal information. About 89 percent of Americans are concerned that their data is being accessed and used inappropriately.

Additionally, the U.S. is one of few democracies in the world that lacks a data protection agency. Senator Gillibrand’s Data Protection Act would create such an agency, strengthening the federal government’s ability to protect Americans’ data and bringing the U.S. in line with peer nations. 

Specifically, the Data Protection Act would:

Limit the collection, use, and sharing of personal data;

Oversee high-risk data practices, ensure that data processing and algorithms are fair, and minimize the collection of data for commercial purposes;

Examine the social, ethical, economic, and civil rights impacts of data collection practices;

Maintain a publicly accessible list of data aggregators that collect, process, or share data;

Enforce privacy statutes and rules as authorized by Congress, with a broad range of tools including civil penalties, injunctive relief, and equitable remedies;

Develop model privacy and data protection standards, guidelines, and policies for use by the private sector and government agencies, and;

Advise Congress on emerging privacy and technology issues.

This legislation is endorsed by the Electronic Privacy Information Center (EPIC), Consumer Federation of America, Fairplay, Consumer Action, and National Association of Consumer Advocates.

“The United States has been ensnared in a data privacy crisis for decades, and putting an end to it will take significant action from Congress,” said Kara Williams, Counsel at the Electronic Privacy Information Center. “EPIC is proud to endorse Sen. Gillibrand’s Data Protection Act, which would establish a federal data protection agency that would focus exclusively on protecting privacy—a crucial first step to ending the mass overcollection and exploitation of Americans’ personal data.” 

“With an increase in surveillance of every corner of life online and off, the need for a strong and clear privacy law with teeth has never been more urgent,” said Ben Winters, Director of AI and Privacy of the Consumer Federation of America. “The Data Protection Act is straightforward, administrable, and what we need right now.” 

“Commercial surveillance has become Silicon Valley’s economic operating system, yet the United States is the only major industrialized country without a dedicated data protection agency to rein in harmful data practices,” said Asad Ramzanali, Director of Artificial Intelligence & Technology Policy at the Vanderbilt Policy Accelerator. “This void leaves Americans exposed and the government underequipped to respond. We’ve long needed a well-staffed watchdog with real authority to enforce privacy rights and hold companies accountable.” 

“Consumers need an agency that makes data protection its priority. Senator Gillibrand’s plan to create a Data Protection Agency is the right step to ensure that companies use individuals’ data fairly, responsibly and with accountability,” said Ruth Susswein, Director of Consumer Protection at Consumer Action. 

“Data centers in the U.S. are vulnerable to attack, and as a country we need to do a much better job with data security. That’s why the U.S. needs a data protection agency,” said Bruce Schneier, Fellow and Lecturer at Harvard Kennedy School.

The full text of the Data Protection Act can be found here.

###

title: Gillibrand, Schumer Pass Legislation To Cement Saratoga Battlefield’s Legacy
text:
Legislation Would Rename Historic Site “Saratoga National Battlefield Park”

Today, U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY) and Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY) announced congressional passage of the bipartisan Strengthening America’s Turning Point Act. This legislation would officially redesignate Saratoga National Historical Park as Saratoga National Battlefield Park, more accurately reflecting its pivotal role in the Revolutionary War.

Representatives Elise Stefanik (R-NY) and Paul Tonko (D-NY) led the legislation in the U.S. House of Representatives, where it passed last year. The bill now heads to the president’s desk.

“Saratoga Battlefield is a source of pride for the Capital Region and a symbol of the patriotism, sacrifice, and resilience that built our country,” said Senator Gillibrand. “The Battles of Saratoga were the turning point of the American Revolution and monumental events in world history, marking the first time that a British army laid down their arms. This name change reflects the historic significance of the battles and honors the sacrifice of those who fought for our nation’s founding.”

“The Battles of Saratoga were the turning point of the American Revolution. I’m proud to announce that legislation renaming the historical park ‘Saratoga National Battlefield Park’ has just passed the Senate and will be signed into law,” said Senator Schumer. “This new name provides important context and reflects the significance of the battlefield as a turning point for the Revolutionary War. As we celebrate America’s 250th anniversary this year, and get ready for the 250th anniversary of the Battles of Saratoga next year, honoring the heart of New York’s Revolutionary War history is key to ensuring America’s history lives on.”

“This summer, as we celebrated our nation’s 250thbirthday, I was reminded once again of the pivotal role our Capital Region played in America’s fight for freedom and independence,” said Rep. Tonko. “Now, as we approach the 250thanniversary of the Battles of Saratoga, I’m thrilled to celebrate the passage through the Senate of the Strengthening America’s Turning Point Act. The designation of ‘Saratoga National Battlefield Park’ will help accurately reflect the importance of this national historic site, boosting local tourism and fostering a greater appreciation for our region’s historic heritage among locals and visitors alike. I was proud last year to lead this legislation through the House, and I’m eager now to see it signed into law.”

The Saratoga National Historical Park is the site of the 1777 Battles of Saratoga, which were some of the first significant American victories over the British army during the Revolutionary War. The battles were called a “turning point” and helped to convince the French to ally with the American colonies. New York State began to preserve the site in 1927. In 1938, Congress passed a law to designate the park as a unit of the National Park System, naming it the “Saratoga National Historical Park.”

Local New York stakeholders have advocated to change the park’s name ahead of the battles’ 250th anniversary to more accurately reflect its significance as a battlefield. In 2024, the Saratoga County Board of Supervisors unanimously adopted a resolution requesting that Congress and the National Park Service change the name. This legislation would finalize this change.

###

title: Gillibrand Statement On New Report That Impending Social Security Benefit Cuts Will Be Deeper Than Predicted
text:
New Report Finds Social Security Benefits Could Be Cut 26% In 2032

Gillibrand’s Social Security Expansion Act Would Extend The Solvency Of Social Security For 75 Years By Requiring The Wealthiest Americans To Pay Their Fair Share Of Payroll Taxes

Following the release of a new report finding that Social Security benefit cuts could be deeper than previously predicted – up to 26% – U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY) slammed the Trump administration for its role in jeopardizing seniors’ benefits and demanded passage of her legislation to extend the solvency and guarantee of Social Security.

“Americans who have worked hard their entire lives deserve every dollar of Social Security they were promised. But due to Trump administration and Republican inaction, their benefits are on track to be slashed by 26% in just six years,” said Senator Gillibrand. “We must take immediate action to prevent this benefit cut. As the top Democrat on the Senate Aging Committee, I’m demanding swift passage of my legislation to blow the Social Security cap, make wealthy Americans pay their fair share, and prevent these draconian benefit cuts.”

This year’s annual Social Security Trustees Report, which was released in June, previously concluded that Social Security’s retirement trust fund will be depleted by 2032. A new Congressional Budget Office (CBO) report released earlier this month concluded that at that time, seniors will see their benefits cut by about 26%–a higher percentage than previously predicted.

Last year, Senator Gillibrand introduced the Social Security Expansion Act to extend the solvency of Social Security for 75 years by requiring the wealthiest American households to pay their fair share of payroll taxes. 

Under the current formula, a CEO making $20 million a year pays the same amount into Social Security as individuals making $184,500 a year. This legislation would lift the cap on Social Security, requiring income above $250,000 to be subject to the Social Security payroll tax and thus increasing the amount paid into the Social Security trust fund to increase its longevity. Under this bill, over 91 percent of American households would not experience a tax increase. 

The full text of this bill can be found here.

The depletion of Social Security funds is due in part to the Trump administration’s reckless policy agenda. The so-called “One Big Beautiful Bill Act,” which was passed by Republicans in Congress and signed into law by President Trump last year, permanently lowered income tax rates. This resulted in less tax being paid on Social Security benefits, reducing the revenue flowing to the Social Security trust fund and decreasing its solvency. At the same time, the administration’s deportation efforts and restrictive immigration policies have further reduced the revenue for the trust fund, as legal immigrants and many undocumented workers pay billions of dollars in Social Security taxes, but undocumented immigrants are not eligible to receive Social Security benefits.

title: Gillibrand Calls Allegations In Cornell Rape Case “Serious And Horrific” On NPR’s All Things Considered
text:
***Hear Senator Gillibrand’s Full Interview Here***

Today, U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY) called the allegations in the Cornell University fraternity rape case “serious and horrific” in an interview on NPR’s All Things Considered and issued the following statement:

“The allegations made in the Cornell University complaint are extremely serious and horrific.

“I am glad the district attorney is reopening this case. Regardless of what this grand jury concludes, the larger truth is clear: a system that forces survivors to these lengths is a system that is fundamentally broken. Victims deserve thorough investigations, and perpetrators must be held accountable.

“Our priorities are upside down. The Senate recently spent two weeks urgently talking about college sports but has spent years looking away from sexual violence and student safety on our college campuses.

“Congress must act and take up my bipartisan Campus Accountability and Safety Act (CASA) with Senator Chuck Grassley to hold campuses accountable, create a fair process for students, and ensure victims have access to a dedicated advocate to assist in navigating the adjudication process.”

Listen to Senator Gillibrand’s interview with NPR here. Full transcript of Senator Gillibrand’s interview below:

SACHA PFEIFFER: It’s All Things Considered from NPR News. I’m Sacha Pfeiffer. 

JUANA SUMMERS: And I’m Juana Summers. When I heard a woman’s allegations that she was drugged and gang raped at a Cornell University fraternity house in 2024, the story felt familiar to me. It’s not because the story was well known before this weekend. It’s because so many of the details she alleges – a campus party, a fraternity, drugs, alcohol, and sexual assault – echo so many of the stories we’ve heard from numerous college campuses for years. 

PFEIFFER: The alleged assault at Cornell happened in 2024. Campus police investigated, but no criminal charges were ever filed. Cornell defends its handling of the case. Now the woman, identified as Jane Doe, has brought a civil case against the university and the seven male students she says assaulted her. That has prompted prosecutors to reopen the case, and the details of these allegations have sparked national outrage. 

SUMMERS: To unpack all of this, I called up someone earlier today who’s been pushing for years for legislation to address the handling of campus sexual assault crimes, New York Democratic Senator Kirsten Gillibrand, and I started by asking her for her reaction to these allegations, as well as the decision to reopen the case. 

GILLIBRAND: Well, I’m certainly grateful that the DA is reopening the investigation. I’ve just seen the public reports, and obviously these allegations are extremely serious and horrific, and as a parent with a kid in college, this is probably something that every parent in America wants addressed. 

SUMMERS: Matthew Van Houten, who’s the Tompkins County District Attorney, said on Monday that Jane Doe’s original statement two years ago, and I’m going to quote him here, did not allege that she was drugged against her will or gang raped. Now, in light of the new details provided in that civil suit, he says he would now let a grand jury decide. Her lawyer told CNN that the new report was not materially different from what was contained in the original complaint. What questions would you want answered about how investigators handled that initial report? 

GILLIBRAND: So, one of the things that I found over the years of working in this space, is that the people who do the interviews initially or ask questions initially have to be highly trained. They have to be experts in this kind of trauma. They have to be experts on what happens when someone has lived through this kind of trauma. You need a trauma-informed counselor to do that first interview, and a lot of our lawyers, a lot of our district attorneys, a lot of law enforcement are not trained in that way. We studied cases where law enforcement groups were trained appropriately, and it exponentially increased the number of people who reported rapes. It increased the number of people whose cases actually went to adjudication, and it increased the number of convictions. 

SUMMERS: I mean, you have been working on these issues for such a long time. I think it was more than a decade ago that I was talking to you, covering the bipartisan push that you and other lawmakers made to address this issue to curb the rates of sexual assaults on campuses. You’ve come back to this legislation over and over again, and yet I have to say, Senator, it doesn’t feel like much has changed. Is that your view? 

GILLIBRAND: No, I think very little has changed. I do imagine that many campuses have put in place much better policies than they had a decade ago, but Congress hasn’t done its part, and we just spent two weeks talking about college sports. Congress should spend at least that time talking about how to make campuses safe for all students. 

SUMMERS: What would you like to see Congress do? What’s an appropriate step here? 

GILLIBRAND: Well, I’d like to have hearings on the piece of legislation that Senator Grassley and I have authored, CASA, and then we should be able to get a vote. Just simply get a vote so that we can hold campuses and communities of responsibility, hold them accountable for whether they are protecting all students or not, and that is literally not happening today on many, many college campuses. 

SUMMERS: Senator Gillibrand, I’ve heard you for a long time, on and off the Hill. So I want to ask you a question, not as a senator, but just as a mom. And I understand that you have at least one son who’s college age. How do you talk to your sons? How do we talk to young men about situations and allegations like these? Because these instances, they keep happening year after year, from college campus to college campus. 

GILLIBRAND: Well, as a mom, I of course worry about the safety and well-being of my children, and I try to make sure that they understand the risks they have every day. I also read the story about a bunch of kids who died on campus because they did some drug that’s not fentanyl but worse than fentanyl. So when I hear stories like this, I just talk to my children about what happened on these campuses, what happened to these children, and ask them like, “Do you ever see yourself in this situation? What would you do in this situation? Who would you ask for help? You know, would you save someone? Would you stick up for someone? Would you prevent someone from taking a risk that’s very scary, like taking drugs?” I think a lot of campuses have some sexual assault prevention training. I don’t know if all campuses have them, but I know that my sons have had those trainings on their campuses. So it’s very hard, and you just want your children and their friends and their whole community to be safe. 

SUMMERS: I mean, just taking a step away from the specifics of these allegations at Cornell University, I just know so many women, myself included, who have had stories of experiencing unwanted sexual contact, assault, or rape on their campuses who then seek help from systems that were ostensibly built to keep them safe, and yet feel let down or betrayed, and it keeps happening. So I guess the question I have is, what makes it stop? What’s the tipping point? 

GILLIBRAND: What you’ve heard from many survivors, and this is the throughline, is that when they felt they could report what happened, they were not received openly. They were received with disbelief. They were received with blame. They were received with, “That’s what you were wearing,” or “You were drinking that,” or “You were doing drugs. What do you expect?” Like sometimes, the first person they talk to is so uninformed and so poorly trained. They say all the wrong things, and the things that they say in those instances often will leave a survivor to drop the case or to blame him or herself and unwilling to tell his or her story. That does not set a campus up for safety or for success. You need to have a system that works, that works for everyone, that is 100% transparent. 

SUMMERS: We’ve been speaking with Democratic Senator Kirsten Gillibrand of New York. Thank you so much. 

GILLIBRAND: Thank you.

###

The post Gillibrand Calls Allegations In Cornell Rape Case “Serious And Horrific” On NPR’s All Things Considered appeared first on Kirsten Gillibrand | U.S. Senator for New York.

title: Gillibrand, Colleagues Press Commissioner Bisignano On Mismanagement, Mistreatment Of Workers At Social Security Administration, IRS
text:
Decision to limit paid annual and sick leave will affect over 120,000 IRS and SSA workers

U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY), ranking member of the Senate Committee on Aging, joined Senators Elizabeth Warren (D-MA), Chris Van Hollen (D-MD), and Ron Wyden (D-OR) in sending a letter to Frank Bisignano, Commissioner of the Social Security Administration (SSA) and Chief Executive Officer of the Internal Revenue Service (IRS), on their concerns about his mistreatment of agency employees after obtaining a circulated internal memo that indicates that he will strip SSA and IRS of advanced annual leave and sick leave.

“The Trump administration has starved the Social Security Administration and the IRS of the resources they need to provide critical services to millions of Americans,” said Senator Gillibrand. “Limiting paid leave will only further push away quality workers from these agencies and cause increased wait times, more frustration, and real hardship for families trying to access essential benefits and file their taxes. I am demanding that the administration immediately reverse this decision and ensure that every American can count on the services they need.”

Workers at the Social Security Administration and the IRS receive advance paid leave policies that allow them to take time off before it is officially accrued, a common practice across the federal workforce. Advanced leave grants employees the ability to respond to health and family emergencies and has long been a part of the federal government’s efforts to provide the workplace conditions needed to attract and retain the most qualified individuals to serve the American people. 

But an internal memorandum indicated that Bisignano, the head of SSA and IRS, would strip agency employees of these benefits.

“We are concerned that this policy will further weaken the already stressed resources of these agencies, leaving the American people with degraded access to their rightful Social Security benefits and needed IRS services,” the senators wrote. “…(Y)ou have imposed a cruel and unjustified plan that is likely to drive additional employees out the door, doubling down on the Administration’s already disastrous efforts to push out federal employees.”

The Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) cut over 32,000 employees from the IRS and the SSA in 2025, diminishing customer service at these agencies. Suspending advanced annual and sick leave will make matters worse, pushing out federal employees and directly hurting Americans who need assistance from the SSA and IRS. These fresh cuts could delay access to benefits and critical tax refunds.

“(T)his latest action to eliminate a workplace benefit could contribute to increasingly dire conditions for agency staff, negatively impacting morale and employee retention and — if the agencies lose additional workers — hurting taxpayers and Social Security recipients,” the senators continued.

The senators urged Bisignano to reverse this decision and immediately restore advanced leave at the SSA and IRS. They further requested that SSA and IRS provide more details on the suspension of advanced paid leave policies at both agencies by no later than October 6, 2026.

As the top Democrat on the Senate Aging Committee, Senator Gillibrand is a staunch supporter of Social Security and has fought the Trump administration’s cuts and overhauls at SSA. In March, she launched an investigation into SSA’s ongoing customer service crisis, after staffing cuts and reassignments left the agency unable to fully serve the 75 million Americans who rely on the program. She has also rallied alongside seniors and unions to demand a reversal of staffing and service cuts, and she pressed SSA on its plans to close field offices and make it harder for Americans to get their benefits.

The full text of the letter is available HERE.
